title: Cyber Fundamentals
description: Foundational cybersecurity knowledge covering networking, cryptography, operating systems, and core security principles required before specializing.

modules.title: Networking Foundations
modules.objective: Explain how data moves across networks using the OSI and TCP/IP models and identify common protocols by port and function.

topics.title: The OSI Model — Seven Layers
concepts: Layer 1 Physical: raw bit transmission over media (copper, fiber, radio)
Layer 2 Data Link: node-to-node frame delivery, MAC addressing, error detection (Ethernet, ARP, switches)
Layer 3 Network: logical addressing, routing between networks (IP, ICMP, routers)
Layer 4 Transport: reliable or unreliable end-to-end delivery (TCP, UDP, port numbers)
Layer 5 Session: managing communication sessions and dialog control
Layer 6 Presentation: data translation, encryption, compression, character encoding
Layer 7 Application: network services to user applications (HTTP, DNS, SMTP)
key_facts: OSI has exactly 7 layers, numbered 1 (bottom/physical) to 7 (top/application)
Mnemonic bottom-up: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away'
Mnemonic top-down: 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing'
Layers 1-3 are 'media layers'; layers 4-7 are 'host layers'
Each layer adds a header (encapsulation); receiving side strips headers (decapsulation)
PDU names: L1=Bits, L2=Frames, L3=Packets, L4=Segments (TCP)/Datagrams (UDP), L7=Data
topics.offense_application: Attackers target specific layers: L2 for ARP spoofing/VLAN hopping, L3 for IP spoofing/routing attacks, L7 for application exploits. Understanding the model helps identify which layer an attack operates at.
topics.defense_application: Defenders map alerts to OSI layers for triage; firewalls operate at L3-L4 (ACLs), WAFs at L7, switches with port security at L2. Layered defense = defense in depth maps directly to OSI layers.
drills: Given a packet capture, identify which OSI layer each header belongs to
Map 10 common protocols to their correct OSI layer numbers
Draw the encapsulation/decapsulation process for an HTTP request through all 7 layers
common_mistakes: Placing ARP at Layer 3 — ARP operates at Layer 2 (Data Link)
Confusing the 5-layer TCP/IP model with the 7-layer OSI model
Thinking encryption only happens at Layer 6 — TLS operates at L6/L7 boundary and encrypts application data

topics.title: The TCP/IP Model
concepts: 4-layer model: Link (Network Interface), Internet, Transport, Application
Maps to OSI: Link=L1+L2, Internet=L3, Transport=L4, Application=L5+L6+L7
Practical model that the actual Internet runs on (RFC 1122)
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, three-way handshake
UDP (User Datagram Protocol): connectionless, unreliable, fast, no handshake
key_facts: TCP/IP has 4 layers vs OSI's 7 layers
TCP uses a 3-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
TCP teardown: FIN, FIN-ACK (or RST for abrupt close)
TCP states: LISTEN, SYN_SENT, SYN_RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT, CLOSE_WAIT, TIME_WAIT
UDP is faster than TCP because it has no handshake, no guaranteed delivery, no ordering
Common TCP protocols: HTTP, HTTPS, SSH, FTP, SMTP; Common UDP protocols: DNS, DHCP, SNMP, NTP, TFTP
topics.offense_application: Attackers exploit TCP state machines for SYN flood DoS, hijack TCP sessions, or prefer UDP for covert channels. C2 frameworks often use TCP but can tunnel over DNS (UDP 53) to evade firewalls.
topics.defense_application: Defenders inspect TCP flags for port scans (SYN scans, XMAS scans, FIN scans), set firewall rules by protocol/port, and use IDS rules to detect anomalous connection patterns like SYN floods.
drills: In Wireshark, trace a full TCP three-way handshake and identify SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK packets
Compare a TCP capture vs UDP capture — identify which has handshake overhead
List which of your system's connections are TCP vs UDP using netstat or ss
common_mistakes: Believing TCP is always better than UDP — UDP is correct for DNS, VoIP, video streaming where speed matters more than retransmission
Confusing the TCP/IP model layers with OSI layer numbers — TCP/IP 'Application' spans OSI layers 5-7
Forgetting that DNS uses both TCP (zone transfers, large responses) and UDP (standard queries)

topics.title: Common Protocols and Port Numbers
concepts: Well-known ports: 0-1023 (require root/admin to bind on Unix)
Registered ports: 1024-49151
Dynamic/ephemeral ports: 49152-65535
IANA assigns and maintains official port numbers
TCP vs UDP port assignments for each protocol
key_facts: FTP: 20 (data), 21 (control) — TCP
SSH: 22 — TCP
Telnet: 23 — TCP (unencrypted!)
SMTP: 25 — TCP (mail transfer between servers)
DNS: 53 — TCP and UDP
DHCP: 67 (server), 68 (client) — UDP
TFTP: 69 — UDP
HTTP: 80 — TCP
Kerberos: 88 — TCP/UDP
POP3: 110 — TCP
NTP: 123 — UDP
RPC Endpoint Mapper: 135 — TCP/UDP
NetBIOS: 137 (Name), 138 (Datagram), 139 (Session) — TCP/UDP
IMAP: 143 — TCP
SNMP: 161 (agent), 162 (trap) — UDP
BGP: 179 — TCP
LDAP: 389 — TCP
HTTPS: 443 — TCP
SMB: 445 — TCP
Syslog: 514 — UDP
SMTP Submission: 587 — TCP
LDAPS: 636 — TCP (LDAP over TLS)
IMAPS: 993 — TCP
POP3S: 995 — TCP
MS SQL Server: 1433 — TCP
MySQL: 3306 — TCP
RDP: 3389 — TCP/UDP
PostgreSQL: 5432 — TCP
WinRM: 5985 (HTTP), 5986 (HTTPS) — TCP
ISAKMP/IKE (IPsec VPN): 500 — UDP
HTTP Alternate: 8080 — TCP
topics.offense_application: Port scanning (Nmap) reveals running services; attackers match open ports to known vulnerabilities (e.g., EternalBlue on SMB 445, BlueKeep on RDP 3389). Insecure protocols like Telnet (23) and FTP (21) transmit credentials in cleartext.
topics.defense_application: Defenders harden by closing unnecessary ports, enforcing least-privilege firewall rules, replacing cleartext protocols (Telnet→SSH, HTTP→HTTPS), and monitoring for unauthorized port usage with tools like netstat, ss, lsof.
drills: Nmap scan a lab machine and identify every open port and its service
Memorize the top 20 ports — quiz yourself on protocol, port number, and TCP/UDP
Identify which ports should never be exposed to the internet (RDP, SMB, NetBIOS, Telnet)
common_mistakes: Thinking port numbers are per-protocol (TCP/UDP) — they are independent; a service can be TCP-only
Assuming a service on port 8080 is always HTTP — many apps use non-standard ports to hide
Forgetting that well-known ports (0-1023) require elevated privileges on Unix-like systems

topics.title: IP Addressing, Subnetting, and CIDR
concepts: IPv4: 32-bit address, 4 octets (0-255 each), ~4.3 billion addresses
IPv6: 128-bit address, 8 groups of hex digits, effectively unlimited addresses
Subnet mask: separates network portion from host portion (e.g., 255.255.255.0 = /24)
CIDR notation: /N means N network bits (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24 = 256 addresses, 254 usable)
NAT (Network Address Translation): translates private IPs to public IPs
Special addresses: 127.0.0.0/8 (loopback), 169.254.0.0/16 (APIPA/link-local), 0.0.0.0 (default route)
key_facts: IPv4 = 32 bits, written as four decimal octets (e.g., 192.168.1.1)
IPv6 = 128 bits, written as eight colon-separated hex groups (e.g., 2001:db8::1)
/24 = 256 total addresses (254 usable hosts), /16 = 65,536 addresses, /8 = 16,777,216 addresses
/30 = 4 addresses (2 usable) — typical for point-to-point links
/31 = 2 addresses — used for point-to-point per RFC 3021
/32 = single host (host route)
Loopback: 127.0.0.1 (IPv4), ::1 (IPv6)
APIPA: 169.254.0.0/16 — assigned when DHCP fails
Number of usable hosts in /N = 2^(32-N) - 2 (subtract network and broadcast addresses)
topics.offense_application: Attackers use subnet knowledge to enumerate internal networks (ping sweeps across /24 ranges), identify network architecture, and pivot through subnets after initial compromise. CIDR ranges guide scanner scope.
topics.defense_application: Defenders segment networks with VLANs and subnets to contain breaches, write precise firewall ACLs using CIDR notation, and design DMZ architectures. Network segmentation limits lateral movement.
drills: Calculate the network address, broadcast address, and host range for 10.20.30.40/22
Given a requirement for 50 hosts per subnet, determine the optimal subnet mask from a /24
Identify whether 172.20.5.10 is a private or public IP and explain why
common_mistakes: Forgetting to subtract 2 from total addresses for network and broadcast addresses
Thinking /24 always means 255.255.255.0 is the only valid mask — it is, but /23, /22 etc. are also common
Confusing NAT with subnetting — NAT translates addresses, subnetting divides address space

topics.title: Routing Fundamentals
concepts: Routers operate at OSI Layer 3 (Network), forward packets between networks
Routing table: destination network, next hop, metric, interface
Default gateway: where packets go when no specific route matches
Static routing: manually configured routes
Dynamic routing protocols: OSPF (Interior), BGP (Exterior/Internet), RIP, EIGRP
BGP: Border Gateway Protocol — routes between autonomous systems (AS), the backbone of the Internet
OSPF: Open Shortest Path First — link-state IGP, uses Dijkstra's algorithm
key_facts: Routers operate at Layer 3; switches at Layer 2
BGP uses TCP port 179
OSPF uses IP protocol number 89 (not TCP or UDP)
RIP uses UDP port 520, max 15 hops (16 = unreachable)
BGP autonomous system numbers (ASN) identify networks on the Internet
Default route is 0.0.0.0/0
topics.offense_application: Attackers manipulate routing tables (ARP spoofing at L2, BGP hijacking at L3) to intercept traffic (MITM), inject malicious routes to redirect traffic, or isolate segments. Route table modification enables traffic interception.
topics.defense_application: Defenders use routing segmentation for isolation, implement route authentication (BGP MD5, OSPF authentication), monitor routing table changes for anomalies, and use ACLs on routing protocol traffic.
drills: Run 'route -n' or 'ip route' and explain every entry in the routing table
Trace the path of a packet from your machine to 8.8.8.8 using traceroute/tracert
Diagram how a packet travels through routers, switches, and the default gateway to reach the internet
common_mistakes: Confusing switches (L2) with routers (L3) — switches forward frames by MAC, routers forward packets by IP
Thinking the default gateway is only for internet traffic — it handles any traffic without a specific route
Forgetting that BGP is what actually runs the Internet's inter-domain routing

modules.title: DNS, HTTP, and Web Protocols in Depth
modules.objective: Explain DNS resolution and HTTP request/response cycles, and identify security weaknesses in both.

topics.title: DNS — Domain Name System in Depth
concepts: DNS translates domain names to IP addresses (forward lookup) and vice versa (reverse lookup)
Hierarchical structure: root (.), TLD (.com, .org), second-level (example.com), subdomains
Resolution process: client → recursive resolver → root server → TLD server → authoritative server
DNS caching at multiple levels (browser, OS, resolver) with TTL (Time To Live)
DNS record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail exchange), TXT (text/SPF/DKIM), NS (name server), SOA (start of authority), PTR (reverse lookup), SRV (service)
key_facts: DNS primarily uses UDP port 53, but TCP port 53 for zone transfers and responses > 512 bytes
A record = IPv4 address; AAAA record (quad-A) = IPv6 address
MX records have priority values (lower = higher priority)
TXT records are used for SPF, DKIM, DMARC email authentication
DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records (using RRSIG, DNSKEY, DS records)
13 logical root server clusters named A through M (a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net)
Common tools: dig, nslookup, host
topics.offense_application: DNS is used for C2 via DNS tunneling (encoding data in subdomain queries), DNS rebinding to bypass same-origin policy, and domain fronting. Attackers compromise DNS to redirect users to phishing sites. DNS exfiltration hides data in DNS queries.
topics.defense_application: Defenders monitor DNS for data exfiltration (long subdomain labels, high entropy queries), implement DNS filtering/blocking (Pi-hole, Cisco Umbrella), enforce DNSSEC to prevent cache poisoning, and use DNS logging as a detection source.
drills: Use 'dig' to manually trace DNS resolution: dig +trace example.com
Query specific record types: dig MX, dig TXT, dig AAAA for a domain
Analyze DNS traffic in Wireshark and identify query/response pairs, record types, and TTL values
common_mistakes: Forgetting DNS can use TCP (not just UDP) for large responses and zone transfers
Thinking DNS is always insecure — DNSSEC exists but adoption is incomplete
Confusing authoritative servers with recursive resolvers — authoritative servers answer for their zones, recursive resolvers chase the chain

topics.title: HTTP and HTTPS
concepts: HTTP: stateless request-response protocol at OSI Layer 7
Request structure: method, URL/path, headers, optional body
Response structure: status line (version, status code, reason), headers, body
HTTPS = HTTP over TLS/SSL — encrypts the entire HTTP message
HTTP/2: multiplexed streams, header compression (HPACK), binary framing
HTTP/3: runs over QUIC (UDP-based), eliminates head-of-line blocking
key_facts: HTTP uses TCP port 80; HTTPS uses TCP port 443
HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections (keep-alive)
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are binary protocols (not human-readable like HTTP/1.1)
HTTP/3 uses UDP (via QUIC) instead of TCP
HTTPS encrypts headers AND body — only the SNI (Server Name Indication) in TLS is visible pre-encryption
Common request headers: Host, User-Agent, Cookie, Authorization, Content-Type, Accept
topics.offense_application: Attackers use HTTP(S) for C2 because it blends with normal web traffic. HTTPS hides payloads from IDS. Web exploits (SQLi, XSS, SSRF) target HTTP requests. Downgrade attacks force HTTPS→HTTP to intercept cleartext.
topics.defense_application: Defenders use TLS inspection (SSL bumping) at proxies, WAFs to inspect Layer 7 HTTP traffic, enforce HSTS to prevent downgrade attacks, and monitor HTTP headers for anomalies. Certificate pinning prevents MITM.
drills: Use curl -v to examine full HTTP request and response headers for a website
Compare HTTP vs HTTPS traffic in Wireshark — show that HTTPS body is encrypted
Identify all HTTP headers in a request and explain what each one does
common_mistakes: Thinking HTTPS encrypts the destination domain — SNI leaks it (only encrypted with ECH/ESNI)
Believing HTTP/2 is human-readable like HTTP/1.1 — HTTP/2 is binary
Forgetting HTTP is stateless — sessions/cookies are workarounds, not built into the protocol

topics.title: Packet Analysis and Network Tools
concepts: Wireshark: GUI packet capture and analysis tool — the industry standard
tcpdump: command-line packet capture tool for servers and embedded systems
pcap/pcapng: packet capture file formats
Display filters vs capture filters (BPF syntax): 'tcp port 443', 'host 192.168.1.1'
Common tools: nmap (port scanning), netcat (network utility), curl (HTTP), dig (DNS), traceroute
Reading packet captures: identifying protocols, TCP handshakes, DNS queries, HTTP requests
TLS decryption: using private keys (RSA) or SSLKEYLOGFILE for session key logging
key_facts: Wireshark display filter syntax: ip.addr==10.0.0.1, tcp.port==443, http.request.method==POST
BPF capture filter syntax (different from display filter): 'tcp port 443', 'host 10.0.0.1'
nmap scan types: -sS (SYN/stealth), -sT (TCP connect), -sU (UDP), -sV (version), -O (OS detection)
netcat (nc): the 'Swiss Army knife' — port scanning, banner grabbing, file transfer, reverse shells
traceroute uses incrementing TTL values (ICMP Time Exceeded messages) to map path
pcap files can be analyzed after capture (offline) or in real-time (live)
Wireshark follows TCP streams to reconstruct full conversations
topics.offense_application: Attackers use packet captures to steal credentials transmitted in cleartext, nmap for reconnaissance and vulnerability identification, and netcat for establishing backdoor connections and data exfiltration.
topics.defense_application: Defenders analyze pcaps to detect intrusions, identify C2 traffic, investigate data exfiltration, verify firewall/IDS rules, and perform network forensics during incident response.
drills: Capture traffic with tcpdump, open the pcap in Wireshark, and identify each protocol layer
Run an nmap scan against a lab machine with -sV and interpret the version detection results
Use Wireshark to follow a TCP stream and reconstruct an HTTP session
common_mistakes: Confusing capture filters (BPF) with display filters (Wireshark) — different syntax entirely
Forgetting that TLS-encrypted traffic cannot be read without the key or SSLKEYLOGFILE
Running full-range nmap scans (-p-) in production — noisy and may trigger alerts

modules.title: Cryptography Fundamentals
modules.objective: Explain symmetric vs asymmetric encryption, hashing, digital signatures, and common cryptographic attacks.

topics.title: Symmetric vs Asymmetric Encryption
concepts: Symmetric encryption: same key for encryption and decryption (shared secret), fast, used for bulk data
Asymmetric encryption: key pair (public + private), slower, used for key exchange and small data
Hybrid encryption: use asymmetric to exchange a symmetric key, then symmetric for bulk data (how TLS works)
Symmetric algorithms: AES, ChaCha20, 3DES (deprecated), DES (obsolete)
Asymmetric algorithms: RSA, ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography), Diffie-Hellman key exchange
key_facts: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard): 128, 192, or 256-bit keys, 128-bit block size — the standard for symmetric encryption
AES-256 is approved for Top Secret data by NSA
RSA: minimum 2048-bit keys recommended; 4096-bit for high security
ECC (P-256 curve): 256-bit ECC key ≈ 3072-bit RSA key in security strength
DES: 56-bit key — broken, obsolete. 3DES: 168-bit effective — deprecated by NIST
ChaCha20: 256-bit key, stream cipher, used in TLS 1.3 as alternative to AES
Symmetric is ~1000x faster than asymmetric for bulk data
AES operates in modes: ECB (insecure!), CBC, GCM (recommended, authenticated), CTR
topics.offense_application: Attackers steal encryption keys (hardcoded in source, in config files, memory dumps), exploit weak algorithms (DES, MD5), and crack symmetric keys with brute force if too short. ECB mode leaks patterns.
topics.defense_application: Defenders enforce strong algorithms (AES-256, RSA-2048+), manage keys in HSMs/KMS, rotate keys regularly, and flag deprecated algorithms (DES, 3DES, RC4) in security scans. Crypto agility allows algorithm migration.
drills: Use OpenSSL to encrypt a file with AES-256-GCM and decrypt it
Generate an RSA 2048-bit key pair and explain the public/private key relationship
Compare the speed of encrypting 100MB with AES vs RSA using OpenSSL benchmarks
common_mistakes: Using ECB mode — identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, leaking patterns (the famous ECB penguin image)
Using DES or 3DES — both deprecated; 3DES has birthday-attack vulnerability at ~2^32 blocks
Thinking longer keys always help — key management and algorithm choice matter more than brute key length

topics.title: Hashing and Message Authentication
concepts: Cryptographic hash: one-way function producing fixed-size output (digest) from any input
Properties: deterministic, pre-image resistant, second pre-image resistant, collision resistant
Hash algorithms: SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-3, BLAKE2/3
Broken hashes: MD5 (collision-broken), SHA-1 (collision-broken — SHAttered 2017)
HMAC: Hash-based Message Authentication Code — hash + secret key for integrity AND authenticity
Password hashing: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2 (with salt and work factor — deliberately slow)
Digital fingerprinting: hashes used for file integrity (checksums) and malware signatures
key_facts: SHA-256 produces a 256-bit (32-byte, 64 hex char) digest
MD5 produces 128-bit — BROKEN for security (collision attacks since 2004)
SHA-1 produces 160-bit — BROKEN (SHAttered collision demonstrated in 2017, Google)
SHA-3 is based on Keccak sponge construction — fundamentally different from SHA-2
Argon2 is the winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition — recommended for password storage
bcrypt has an adaptive work factor (cost parameter) — can be increased as hardware improves
Salt: random value added to password before hashing — prevents rainbow table attacks
Pepper: secret key added alongside salt — stored separately, unknown to the database
topics.offense_application: Attackers use rainbow tables and GPU hash cracking (hashcat, John the Ripper) against unsalted/weakly hashed passwords. MD5 collisions enable certificate forgery. Hash collisions allow creating two different files with the same hash.
topics.defense_application: Defenders use bcrypt/Argon2 for password storage with unique salts, verify file integrity with SHA-256 checksums (tripwire, AIDE), detect malware via hash signatures, and migrate away from MD5/SHA-1 everywhere.
drills: Hash a file with SHA-256 using sha256sum, modify one byte, and hash again — observe avalanche effect
Crack a list of unsalted MD5 hashes vs bcrypt hashes using hashcat — compare difficulty
Generate an HMAC for a message and verify it using OpenSSL
common_mistakes: Using MD5 or SHA-1 for security-critical purposes (certificates, password storage, integrity)
Storing passwords as plain SHA-256 without salt or work factor — GPU-crackable in seconds
Confusing encoding (Base64) with encryption or hashing — Base64 is reversible, hashing is not

topics.title: Digital Signatures
concepts: Digital signature: hash of data encrypted with sender's private key
Verification: decrypt signature with sender's public key, compare to hash of received data
Provides: authentication (who sent it), integrity (not modified), non-repudiation (cannot deny sending)
Signature algorithms: RSA-PSS, ECDSA, EdDSA (Ed25519)
Distinct from HMAC: signatures use asymmetric keys, HMAC uses a shared symmetric key
Code signing: software developers sign executables so users can verify authenticity
key_facts: ECDSA with P-256 is the NIST-recommended curve for digital signatures
Ed25519 is preferred in modern systems — faster, resistant to side-channel attacks, deterministic
RSA signatures: minimum 2048-bit, 3072-bit recommended for long-term
Digital signatures do NOT provide confidentiality — encrypt separately if needed
Sign-then-encrypt vs encrypt-then-sign — encrypt-then-sign is generally preferred
TLS 1.3 dropped RSA key exchange and uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (forward secrecy)
topics.offense_application: Attackers steal code-signing certificates to sign malware (appears legitimate to AV/OS). Stolen private keys allow impersonation. ECDSA nonce reuse leaks private keys (Sony PlayStation 3 hack).
topics.defense_application: Defenders verify digital signatures on software (GPG, Authenticode), implement certificate-based authentication (smart cards, mutual TLS), and use signed firmware updates. Code signing prevents supply-chain attacks.
drills: Sign a file with GPG and verify the signature — explain the math (hash + private key)
Examine a code-signed Windows executable's signature using sigcheck or Get-AuthenticodeSignature
Explain why you must sign-then-encrypt for both confidentiality and non-repudiation
common_mistakes: Confusing digital signatures with encryption — signatures prove authenticity/integrity, not confidentiality
Thinking signatures provide non-repudiation with symmetric keys — true non-repudiation requires asymmetric keys
Reusing the ECDSA nonce (k) — catastrophic: leaks the private key completely

modules.title: PKI, Certificates, and TLS
modules.objective: Explain how PKI and the TLS handshake establish secure encrypted channels, and identify common cryptographic attacks.

topics.title: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) and X.509 Certificates
concepts: PKI: framework of roles, policies, and procedures for managing digital certificates
Certificate Authority (CA): trusted entity that issues and signs certificates
Registration Authority (RA): verifies identity before certificate issuance
Certificate Revocation List (CRL) and OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol): revocation checking
X.509 certificate format: subject, issuer, public key, validity dates, extensions, CA signature
Chain of trust: root CA → intermediate CA → end-entity certificate
Certificate Transparency (CT): public logs of all issued certificates for accountability
key_facts: X.509 is the standard certificate format (v3 is current)
Root CA certificates are self-signed and pre-installed in OS/browser trust stores
OCSP uses HTTP (port 80 typically) to check revocation status in real-time
CRL is a signed list of revoked certificate serial numbers
Common certificate extensions: SAN (Subject Alternative Name), Key Usage, Extended Key Usage
Certificate pinning: hardcoding expected public key to prevent CA compromise MITM
Let's Encrypt provides free automated DV (Domain Validation) certificates
EV (Extended Validation) certificates show organization name (green bar, deprecated in browsers)
topics.offense_application: Attackers compromise CAs to issue fraudulent certificates (DigiNotar breach 2011), steal private keys from servers, and exploit OCSP stapling issues. Rogue CA certificates in trust stores enable undetectable MITM.
topics.defense_application: Defenders enforce certificate pinning for critical apps, monitor Certificate Transparency logs for unauthorized certificates, rotate certificates regularly, use HSTS to prevent certificate bypass, and maintain private PKI for internal infrastructure.
drills: Examine a website's certificate chain in a browser — identify root CA, intermediate CA, and leaf certificate
Use OpenSSL to generate a CSR (Certificate Signing Request), sign it with a local CA, and install it
Check a certificate's OCSP status and CRL for revocation
common_mistakes: Trusting a certificate without verifying the full chain up to a root CA
Ignoring certificate expiration — expired certificates cause outages and security warnings
Assuming HTTPS = secure — a valid certificate only proves identity, not that the server is safe

topics.title: The TLS Handshake
concepts: TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts application-layer data (replaced SSL)
TLS handshake: negotiate cipher suite, authenticate server via certificate, derive shared keys
Forward secrecy (PFS): session keys are ephemeral — compromise of long-term key doesn't decrypt past sessions
TLS 1.2: ClientHello, ServerHello, Certificate, Key Exchange, ChangeCipherSpec, Finished (2 RTT)
TLS 1.3: streamlined handshake (1 RTT or 0-RTT with resumption), removed RSA key exchange, mandated PFS
Cipher suite components: key exchange, authentication, encryption, MAC/hash
key_facts: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) is the current standard — deprecated TLS 1.0 and 1.1 in 2020
TLS 1.2 requires 2 round trips (2-RTT); TLS 1.3 requires only 1-RTT (or 0-RTT with PSK)
TLS 1.3 removed: RSA key exchange, static DH, CBC mode, SHA-1, RC4, MD5
TLS 1.3 requires: ephemeral DH (DHE/ECDHE) for forward secrecy, AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305)
TLS 1.3 cipher suites are simpler: only 5 approved suites (e.g., TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384)
SNI (Server Name Indication): client tells server which hostname it wants — visible before encryption (privacy leak)
ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) encrypts SNI to fix the privacy leak
SSL 3.0 (POODLE attack), TLS 1.0 (BEAST attack) — both deprecated
topics.offense_application: Attackers perform downgrade attacks (forcing TLS 1.0/SSLv3 to enable BEAST/POODLE), exploit certificate validation flaws, and intercept without forward secrecy if they capture traffic and later obtain the private key.
topics.defense_application: Defenders disable TLS 1.0/1.1, enforce TLS 1.2+, prefer TLS 1.3, use HSTS to prevent downgrade, enable OCSP stapling, and scan for weak cipher suites with tools like testssl.sh and SSL Labs.
drills: Capture a TLS 1.2 handshake in Wireshark and label each message (ClientHello, ServerHello, Certificate, etc.)
Use SSL Labs (ssllabs.com) to test a website's TLS configuration and identify weaknesses
Compare a TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3 handshake — count the round trips
common_mistakes: Enabling TLS 1.0/1.1 'for compatibility' — these are deprecated and vulnerable
Allowing CBC mode ciphers in TLS 1.2 — prefer GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 (AEAD)
Thinking HTTPS means forward secrecy — only TLS 1.3 mandates it; TLS 1.2 needs ECDHE cipher suites

topics.title: Common Cryptographic Attacks
concepts: Man-in-the-Middle (MITM): attacker intercepts and possibly modifies communication between two parties
Downgrade attack: forcing use of weaker protocol/cipher (e.g., POODLE, Logjam)
Padding oracle attack: exploiting error messages about padding to decrypt ciphertext (POODLE, Lucky 13)
Birthday attack: exploiting collision probability (birthday paradox) — affects hashes at 2^(n/2) complexity
Brute force: trying all possible keys — mitigated by sufficient key length
Side-channel attacks: timing, power analysis, cache timing to extract keys
Replay attack: capturing and resending valid messages
key_facts: POODLE (2014): exploits SSL 3.0 CBC padding — downgrade to SSLv3 to decrypt cookies
BEAST (2011): exploits TLS 1.0 CBC mode — fixed in TLS 1.1+
Logjam (2015): exploits weak DH key exchange — downgrade to export-grade 512-bit DH
Heartbleed (2014): OpenSSL bug (CVE-2014-0160) leaks memory including private keys
Lucky 13: timing attack on TLS CBC mode padding verification
Spectre/Meltdown (2018): CPU side-channel attacks that can leak cryptographic keys from memory
Birthday paradox: for n-bit hash, collision found in ~2^(n/2) operations (SHA-256 → 2^128)
Replay attacks prevented by nonces, timestamps, and sequence numbers
topics.offense_application: Attackers downgrade connections to exploit older protocols, use padding oracles to decrypt cookies byte-by-byte, capture HTTPS traffic now and crack it later if no forward secrecy, and exploit implementation bugs like Heartbleed to steal keys.
topics.defense_application: Defenders disable legacy protocols (SSLv3, TLS 1.0), use AEAD ciphers (no padding oracle), enforce forward secrecy, patch crypto libraries promptly (Heartbleed patching), and use HSTS to prevent downgrades.
drills: Research the Heartbleed vulnerability — explain how the heartbeat extension bug leaks memory
Demonstrate a MITM using ettercap or bettercap in a lab environment on HTTP traffic
Check a server's TLS configuration for downgrade vulnerability using testssl.sh
common_mistakes: Assuming strong algorithms are enough — implementation bugs (Heartbleed) and configuration errors (weak ciphers enabled) are more common than algorithm breaks
Ignoring side-channel attacks in high-security environments — timing attacks can extract keys remotely
Believing longer keys protect against protocol-level attacks like downgrades

modules.title: Linux Fundamentals for Security
modules.objective: Navigate the Linux file system, manage permissions and processes, and understand systemd from both attack and defense perspectives.

topics.title: Linux File System Structure
concepts: Everything is a file (devices, processes, network connections via /proc)
Root directory: / — hierarchical tree structure
Key directories: /bin, /sbin, /etc, /home, /var, /tmp, /opt, /usr, /proc, /sys, /dev
/etc: system configuration files (passwd, shadow, hosts, ssh/sshd_config)
/var/log: system and application logs (auth.log, syslog, messages)
/proc: virtual filesystem exposing kernel and process info (PID, /proc/self)
/dev: device files (null, zero, random, urandom, sda, tty)
File paths: absolute (/etc/passwd) vs relative (../config)
key_facts: /etc/passwd: user account info (readable by all), /etc/shadow: password hashes (root-only)
/etc/shadow format: username:$hash:fields — $6$ = SHA-512, $2b$ = bcrypt
/var/log/auth.log (Debian/Ubuntu) or /var/log/secure (RHEL/CentOS): authentication logs
/proc/1/cmdline: command line of PID 1 (usually systemd)
/dev/null discards data, /dev/zero produces null bytes, /dev/urandom produces random bytes
Hidden files start with . (dotfiles like .bashrc, .ssh)
Symlinks (ln -s) vs hard links (ln)
topics.offense_application: Attackers read /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow for credentials, enumerate /home for SSH keys and bash history, search config files for hardcoded passwords, and read /proc to find process details and network connections.
topics.defense_application: Defenders restrict file permissions on sensitive files, use file integrity monitoring (AIDE, tripwire) on /etc and binaries, audit access to sensitive paths, and monitor /var/log for unauthorized access attempts.
drills: Navigate the entire Linux directory tree and explain the purpose of each top-level directory
Read /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow — identify the format and why shadow is root-only
Use /proc to find all network connections of a process without netstat
common_mistakes: Thinking /etc/passwd contains password hashes — they moved to /etc/shadow in modern Linux
Confusing /tmp (world-writable, ephemeral) with /var/tmp (persists across reboots)
Ignoring /proc and /sys — these virtual filesystems are goldmines for process and kernel information

topics.title: Linux Users, Groups, and Permissions
concepts: Three permission types: read (r=4), write (w=2), execute (x=1)
Three permission scopes: owner (user), group, others (world)
Octal notation: rwxr-xr-x = 755, rw-r--r-- = 644, rwxrwxrwx = 777
chmod: change permissions (symbolic: chmod u+x, or octal: chmod 755)
chown: change owner, chgrp: change group
SUID (Set User ID): run executable as file owner (e.g., sudo, passwd command)
SGID (Set Group ID): run as group owner; on directories, new files inherit group
Sticky bit: only file owner can delete files in directory (e.g., /tmp)
key_facts: Permission octal values: r=4, w=2, x=1 — sum them per scope (0-7 each)
SUID = 4000 octal, SGID = 2000 octal, Sticky bit = 1000 octal
/tmp typically has sticky bit (drwxrwxrwt = 1777) — users can only delete their own files
SUID binaries are privilege escalation vectors — find with: find / -perm -4000
Common SUID binaries: sudo, su, passwd, mount, ping, nmap (sometimes)
root (UID 0) bypasses all permission checks
umask determines default permissions for new files (e.g., 022 → files: 644, dirs: 755)
topics.offense_application: Attackers exploit SUID/SGID binaries for privilege escalation (GTFOBins), search for world-readable sensitive files, abuse misconfigured sudo permissions (sudo -l), and modify file permissions after gaining access.
topics.defense_application: Defenders audit SUID binaries regularly, enforce strict permissions on sensitive files, use AppArmor/SELinux for mandatory access control, monitor for unauthorized permission changes, and harden sudo configurations.
drills: Find all SUID binaries on a system with 'find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null' and evaluate each
Set permissions on a script to 750, then explain what each digit means
Run 'sudo -l' and identify any overly permissive sudo rules that could enable privilege escalation
common_mistakes: Using chmod 777 on files/directories — grants world write access, a major security risk
Forgetting about SUID/SGID binaries when auditing security — these are common privesc vectors
Thinking file permissions protect against root — root bypasses standard Unix permissions entirely

topics.title: Processes and Systemd
concepts: Process: running instance of a program, identified by PID (Process ID)
Process hierarchy: init/systemd (PID 1) → child processes → grandchildren
Foreground vs background processes, signals (SIGTERM=15, SIGKILL=9, SIGHUP=1)
systemd: modern init system and service manager (replaced SysV init)
systemd units: .service, .timer, .socket, .mount, .target
journalctl: query systemd journal for centralized logging
Daemons: background services (named with 'd' suffix — sshd, httpd, crond)
Cron: scheduled task execution (crontab, /etc/cron.*)
key_facts: systemd is PID 1 on most modern Linux distributions (since ~2015)
Common systemd commands: systemctl start/stop/enable/disable/status <service>
journalctl -u <service>: view logs for a specific service
journalctl -f: follow logs in real-time (like tail -f)
Process states: Running (R), Sleeping (S), Disk Sleep (D), Stopped (T), Zombie (Z)
Zombie process: child finished but parent hasn't read exit status
Signals: SIGTERM (15, graceful), SIGKILL (9, force kill, cannot be caught), SIGHUP (1, reload config)
Cron format: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week (e.g., */5 * * * * = every 5 minutes)
topics.offense_application: Attackers create malicious systemd services or cron jobs for persistence, hide processes by renaming them, inject into legitimate processes, and use systemd timers as stealthy scheduled tasks.
topics.defense_application: Defenders enumerate running processes (ps aux, top), inspect systemd services for unauthorized entries, audit cron jobs, use process monitoring (auditd, sysmon-for-linux), and detect anomalous parent-child process relationships.
drills: Create a simple systemd service file, enable it, start it, and check its status with systemctl and journalctl
List all running processes and identify their parent PIDs — trace the tree back to PID 1
Audit all cron jobs on a system (crontab -l for each user + /etc/cron.*) for suspicious entries
common_mistakes: Killing processes with SIGKILL (-9) by default — use SIGTERM (-15) first for graceful shutdown
Ignoring systemd timers — attackers increasingly use .timer units instead of cron for persistence
Confusing enable (start on boot) with start (run now) in systemctl

modules.title: Windows Internals for Security
modules.objective: Navigate Windows internals including the registry, services, Active Directory, and event logs for both attack and defense.

topics.title: Windows Registry
concepts: Registry: hierarchical database storing Windows configuration settings
Five root keys: HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT (HKCR), HKEY_CURRENT_USER (HKCU), HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (HKLM), HKEY_USERS (HKU), HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG (HKCC)
Registry structure: keys → subkeys → values (name, type, data)
Common value types: REG_SZ (string), REG_DWORD (32-bit int), REG_BINARY, REG_EXPAND_SZ, REG_MULTI_SZ
Persistence locations: Run keys, Winlogon, Services, Scheduled Tasks, WMI
Tools: regedit (GUI), reg (command line), PowerShell (Get-ItemProperty, Set-ItemProperty)
key_facts: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run — classic autorun persistence location
HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run — per-user persistence
HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet — services and drivers
HKLM\SAM — Security Account Manager (password hashes, restricted access)
HKLM\SECURITY — full security database (domain cache, LSA secrets)
Registry hives stored as files: NTUSER.DAT (HKCU), SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SAM, SECURITY (in C:\Windows\System32\config\)
RegRipper and RECmd are forensic tools for registry analysis
topics.offense_application: Attackers add entries to Run keys for persistence, modify registry to disable security features (Windows Defender, UAC), install registry-based COM hijacking, and read SAM hive for password hashes (needs SYSTEM access).
topics.defense_application: Defenders monitor registry changes (Sysmon Event ID 12/13/14), check known persistence locations during incident response, use registry ACLs, and baseline known-good registry state for comparison.
drills: Navigate to the Run keys in regedit and explain what programs start at login
Use 'reg query' from command line to read a registry value
Use Sysmon to monitor registry modifications and identify Run key changes
common_mistakes: Editing HKLM without admin privileges — requires elevated rights
Forgetting that HKCU is per-user — malware in HKCU only runs for that user, not system-wide
Ignoring registry as a persistence mechanism during incident response

topics.title: Windows Services, Processes, and WMI
concepts: Windows services: background processes managed by Service Control Manager (SCM)
Service types: own process, shared process, kernel driver
Service accounts: LocalSystem (SYSTEM), LocalService, NetworkService
WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation): management infrastructure for querying and controlling Windows
Task Manager and Process Explorer for process analysis
Critical system processes: System, smss.exe, csrss.exe, wininit.exe, services.exe, svchost.exe, lsass.exe, winlogon.exe
svchost.exe hosts multiple Windows services — legitimate but also impersonated by malware
key_facts: SCM (Service Control Manager) runs as services.exe
svchost.exe should always run from C:\Windows\System32\ and be signed by Microsoft
lsass.exe (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service): handles authentication, stores credentials — prime target for credential dumping (Mimikatz)
WMI permanent event subscriptions are a stealthy persistence mechanism
Service commands: sc query, sc config, Get-Service, Start-Service (PowerShell)
WMIC (deprecated) and PowerShell CIM cmdlets (Get-CimInstance) for WMI queries
Event IDs 7045 (new service), 7036 (service state change) in System log
topics.offense_application: Attackers create malicious services for persistence and privilege escalation (if service runs as SYSTEM), use WMI for lateral movement and stealthy execution, and target lsass.exe for credential dumping with Mimikatz.
topics.defense_application: Defenders monitor service creation (Event ID 7045), verify svchost.exe paths and parent processes, protect lsass.exe with Credential Guard and RunAsPPL, and detect WMI event subscriptions.
drills: Use Process Explorer to identify the parent-child relationships of all running svchost.exe instances
List all running services with 'Get-Service' and identify which run as LocalSystem
Query WMI for running processes using PowerShell: Get-CimInstance Win32_Process
common_mistakes: Assuming all svchost.exe processes are legitimate — malware commonly impersonates it
Ignoring the security implications of services running as LocalSystem (full admin)
Forgetting to protect lsass.exe — it's the #1 target for credential theft

topics.title: Active Directory Fundamentals
concepts: Active Directory (AD): Microsoft's directory service for Windows domain networks
Domain Controller (DC): server running AD, authenticates users and stores directory data
AD structure: Forest > Domain > Organizational Units (OUs) > Objects (users, computers, groups)
Objects: users, computers, groups, service accounts, GPOs (Group Policy Objects)
Authentication: primarily Kerberos (port 88) for domain logon, NTLM as fallback
LDAP (port 389/636): protocol for querying and modifying AD directory data
Trust relationships: between domains and forests
Group Policy (GPO): centralized configuration management pushed to domain machines
key_facts: AD uses DNS for service location (SRV records, _ldap._tcp.domain.com)
Kerberos is the default authentication protocol (port 88 TCP/UDP)
LDAP operates on port 389 (TCP), LDAPS on port 636 (TCP)
SMB (port 445) used for SYSVOL replication and file sharing
Global Catalog: searchable index of all objects in the forest (port 3268/3269)
Common AD attack tools: BloodHound (attack path mapping), PowerView (enumeration), Mimikatz
Key AD attacks: Kerberoasting, AS-REP Roasting, Pass-the-Hash, Golden Ticket, Silver Ticket
Domain Admin is the most privileged group — compromise = full domain control
topics.offense_application: Attackers enumerate AD for attack paths (BloodHound), extract service account tickets (Kerberoasting), forge Kerberos tickets (Golden/Silver Ticket), pass hashes between machines, and abuse GPOs for lateral movement.
topics.defense_application: Defenders use BloodHound defensively to identify and close attack paths, enforce tiered admin model, protect KRBTGT account, monitor for anomalous Kerberos ticket requests, implement LAPS for local admin password management, and use managed service accounts (gMSA).
drills: In a lab AD environment, use BloodHound to map attack paths from a standard user to Domain Admin
Enumerate all service accounts in AD using PowerShell (Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null'})
Explain the difference between Golden Ticket (forged TGT using KRBTGT hash) and Silver Ticket (forged service ticket using service account hash)
common_mistakes: Giving too many users Domain Admin privileges — should be extremely limited (tier 0)
Using regular user accounts as service accounts — use gMSAs instead to avoid Kerberoasting
Forgetting that compromising a Domain Controller means total domain compromise

topics.title: Windows Event Logs and Auditing
concepts: Windows Event Log: centralized logging of system, security, and application events
Event Viewer: GUI tool for browsing logs; channels: Application, Security, System, Setup, Forwarded Events
Event ID: numeric identifier for specific event types
Sysmon (System Monitor): advanced host monitoring tool from Sysinternals — goes beyond default logging
PowerShell Event Log: Module, ScriptBlock, and Provider logs
Windows Audit Policy: defines what security events are logged
WEF (Windows Event Forwarding): centralized log collection to a collector
key_facts: Event ID 4624: successful logon; 4625: failed logon
Event ID 4648: explicit credential logon (RunAs); 4672: special privileges assigned
Event ID 4688: process creation (requires audit process creation enabled)
Event ID 7045: new service installed (System log)
Logon types: 2 (Interactive), 3 (Network), 7 (Unlock), 10 (RemoteInteractive/RDP), 5 (Service)
Sysmon Event ID 1: process creation, 3: network connection, 7: image loaded (DLL), 10: process access, 11: file creation, 13: registry value set, 22: DNS query
PowerShell ScriptBlock logging: Event ID 4104 (reveals script content even when obfuscated)
Get-WinEvent and Get-EventLog: PowerShell cmdlets for querying logs
topics.offense_application: Attackers clear or tamper with event logs (Event ID 1102 — audit log cleared), disable Sysmon or audit policies, use living-off-the-land binaries to minimize logged events, and clear PowerShell history.
topics.defense_application: Defenders forward logs to a SIEM (Splunk, ELK) for centralized analysis, deploy Sysmon with a robust config (SwiftOnSecurity), monitor for log clearing (Event ID 1102), set up alerts on key event IDs, and enable PowerShell ScriptBlock logging.
drills: Install Sysmon with SwiftOnSecurity config and generate/test Event IDs 1, 3, and 11
Query Security log for Event ID 4624 and identify the logon type for each entry
Set up a PowerShell ScriptBlock logging alert that triggers on suspicious commands
common_mistakes: Not enabling Sysmon — default Windows logging misses many important events
Forgetting PowerShell logging — ScriptBlock logging catches obfuscated and encoded PowerShell
Only looking at Security log — Application and System logs also contain critical security events

modules.title: Identity and Access Management
modules.objective: Distinguish authentication from authorization and explain modern identity protocols including OAuth, OIDC, SAML, and Kerberos.

topics.title: Authentication vs Authorization
concepts: Authentication (AuthN): verifying WHO you are (proving identity)
Authorization (AuthZ): determining WHAT you can do (permissions/access rights)
Accounting/Auditing: tracking what you did (logs, audit trails)
AAA: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting — the three pillars
Identification: claiming an identity (username) — must be authenticated before trusted
AuthN factors: something you know (password), something you have (token), something you are (biometric)
AuthZ models: DAC (Discretionary), MAC (Mandatory), RBAC (Role-Based), ABAC (Attribute-Based)
key_facts: Authentication = identity verification; Authorization = permission check
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires 2+ different factor types (not 2 passwords)
NIST SP 800-63B: passwords should be long, not necessarily complex; no mandatory periodic rotation for good passwords
Something you know: password, PIN, security question
Something you have: smart card, hardware token (YubiKey), phone (TOTP app)
Something you are: fingerprint, face, iris, voice (biometrics)
RBAC: permissions assigned to roles, users assigned to roles
ABAC: permissions based on attributes (user, resource, environment) — more granular than RBAC
topics.offense_application: Attackers steal credentials (phishing, brute force, credential dumping) to authenticate, exploit broken authorization (IDOR, privilege escalation), bypass MFA (SIM swapping, MFA fatigue/prompt bombing), and use stolen session tokens to skip authentication entirely.
topics.defense_application: Defenders enforce MFA everywhere, implement least-privilege RBAC/ABAC, monitor for impossible travel and anomalous logins, use conditional access policies, implement session timeouts, and audit permission creep.
drills: Design an RBAC model for a small company: list roles, users, and permissions
Identify which factors each of your accounts uses and whether they are truly multi-factor
Explain how an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) is an authorization failure, not an authentication failure
common_mistakes: Using two passwords as 'two-factor' — same factor type (something you know) is single-factor
Confusing authentication with authorization — a properly authenticated user can still be unauthorized
Implementing authorization checks only at login — checks needed at every resource access

topics.title: OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, and SAML
concepts: OAuth 2.0: authorization framework — delegates access without sharing credentials (access tokens)
OpenID Connect (OIDC): authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 (ID tokens, JWT)
SAML 2.0: XML-based SSO protocol for enterprise federation (used by ADFS, Okta)
OAuth roles: Resource Owner, Client, Authorization Server, Resource Server
OAuth grant types: authorization code, client credentials, device code, PKCE (mobile/SPA)
Tokens: access token (API authorization), refresh token (get new access token), ID token (OIDC identity claims)
JWT (JSON Web Token): compact, self-contained token format (header.payload.signature)
key_facts: OAuth 2.0 is for AUTHORIZATION, not authentication — OIDC adds authentication
OIDC returns an ID token (JWT) with user identity claims (sub, email, name)
SAML uses XML, OAuth/OIDC uses JSON — SAML is older, more enterprise-focused
Authorization Code flow with PKCE is recommended for all client types (RFC 9700)
Implicit flow is DEPRECATED — use Authorization Code + PKCE instead
JWT structure: header.payload.signature, base64url-encoded, signed (typically RS256 or ES256)
JWT is NOT encrypted by default — don't put secrets in JWT claims
Common OAuth attacks: stolen authorization codes, open redirects, weak redirect URI validation, token replay
topics.offense_application: Attackers steal OAuth access/refresh tokens (phishing via OAuth consent prompts — 'illicit consent grant'), forge JWTs (algorithm confusion: none/HS256/RS256), exploit open redirect vulnerabilities in OAuth flows, and abuse overly permissive API scopes.
topics.defense_application: Defenders validate JWT signatures server-side, enforce strict redirect URI allowlists, use PKCE, implement token expiration and rotation, audit OAuth consent grants, and monitor for suspicious token usage patterns.
drills: Decode a JWT at jwt.io — inspect header, payload, and signature — identify the signing algorithm
Trace an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code + PKCE flow step by step and explain each request/response
Explain why the implicit flow was deprecated and how PKCE solves the problem it was meant for
common_mistakes: Using OAuth 2.0 for authentication without OIDC — OAuth alone doesn't verify identity
Accepting JWT with 'alg: none' — always verify signatures and reject unsigned tokens
Storing sensitive data in JWT claims — JWT payload is base64-encoded, NOT encrypted

topics.title: Kerberos Authentication Protocol
concepts: Kerberos: network authentication protocol using symmetric key cryptography and tickets
Key Distribution Center (KDC): consists of Authentication Server (AS) and Ticket Granting Server (TGS)
AS-REQ/AS-REP: initial authentication — user gets Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT)
TGS-REQ/TGS-REP: user presents TGT to get service ticket for specific service
Service ticket: presented to target service for authentication
SPN (Service Principal Name): uniquely identifies a service instance in AD
In Active Directory, the KDC runs on Domain Controllers; KRBTGT account's hash encrypts TGTs
key_facts: Kerberos uses port 88 (TCP/UDP) and port 464 for password change
TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) is encrypted with the KRBTGT account's hash — user can't read contents
Service tickets are encrypted with the service account's hash
Tickets have lifetimes: TGT typically 10 hours (renewable up to 7 days in AD)
Kerberoasting: request service tickets for SPN-bearing accounts, crack offline (tickets contain encrypted material using service account's hash)
AS-REP Roasting: targets accounts with 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' — offline crackable AS-REP
Golden Ticket: forged TGT using stolen KRBTGT hash — full domain access until TGT lifetime expires
Silver Ticket: forged service ticket using service account hash — access to specific service
topics.offense_application: Attackers perform Kerberoasting (request and crack service tickets), AS-REP Roasting (crack AS-REP for accounts without preauth), Pass-the-Ticket (reuse stolen tickets), Golden Ticket (forge TGT with KRBTGT hash), and Silver Ticket (forge service ticket).
topics.defense_application: Defenders use strong passwords/gMSAs for service accounts (resistant to Kerberoasting), disable 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication', protect KRBTGT account (rotate password twice after compromise), monitor for anomalous TGS requests, and use AES encryption for Kerberos.
drills: Trace the Kerberos authentication flow: user → AS → TGT → TGS → service ticket → service
Explain why Kerberoasting works offline — the service ticket is encrypted with the service account hash, crackable without contacting the DC
Describe how a Golden Ticket differs from a Silver Ticket and what hash each requires
common_mistakes: Confusing TGT (issued by AS, encrypted with KRBTGT hash) with service ticket (issued by TGS, encrypted with service account hash)
Forgetting that Kerberos requires time synchronization — tickets have timestamps and clocks must be within 5 minutes
Using weak passwords for service accounts — makes Kerberoasted tickets trivially crackable

topics.title: MFA, SSO, and Directory Services
concepts: MFA: requiring multiple authentication factors from different categories
TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password): Google Authenticator, Authy — RFC 6238, 30-second window
HOTP (HMAC-based OTP): counter-based OTP — RFC 4226
FIDO2/WebAuthn: hardware-based authentication resistant to phishing (public key challenge-response)
SSO (Single Sign-On): one login grants access to multiple applications (SAML, OIDC)
Directory services: LDAP, Active Directory, Entra ID (Azure AD), Okta, FreeIPA
Conditional access: policy-based access control considering user, device, location, risk
key_facts: TOTP codes change every 30 seconds and are derived from a shared secret + current time
FIDO2/WebAuthn is phishing-resistant — private key never leaves the device, origin-bound
SMS-based MFA is the weakest — vulnerable to SIM swapping
Common SSO protocols: SAML 2.0 (enterprise), OIDC (modern apps), WS-Federation (legacy Microsoft)
Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is Microsoft's cloud-based directory service
LDAP distinguished names (DN): CN=user,OU=IT,DC=example,DC=com
MFA fatigue attack: sending repeated push notifications hoping user approves one
topics.offense_application: Attackers bypass MFA via SIM swapping (SMS), MFA fatigue (push bombing), adversary-in-the-middle (reverse proxy phishing kits like Evilginx), steal session cookies post-MFA, and downgrade to weaker authentication methods.
topics.defense_application: Defenders prefer FIDO2/hardware keys over SMS/TOTP, implement number matching for push MFA (prevents fatigue attacks), monitor for new device registrations, use conditional access with device compliance checks, and implement risk-based authentication.
drills: Compare security of SMS MFA vs TOTP vs FIDO2 against phishing, SIM swap, and MITM attacks
Set up a TOTP MFA app and explain the shared secret and time window
Explain how an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kit defeats traditional MFA but not FIDO2
common_mistakes: Relying on SMS for MFA in high-security environments — SIM swapping is common
Implementing push MFA without number matching — vulnerable to fatigue attacks
Thinking MFA makes phishing impossible — AiTM phishing kits intercept both credentials and MFA

modules.title: Core Security Principles and Architecture
modules.objective: Apply fundamental security principles including the CIA triad, least privilege, defense in depth, and zero trust to real-world scenarios.

topics.title: The CIA Triad
concepts: Confidentiality: information is accessible only to authorized parties (encryption, access control)
Integrity: information is accurate and unaltered (hashing, digital signatures, version control)
Availability: information and systems are accessible when needed (redundancy, backups, DDoS protection)
Every security control maps to at least one CIA component
Tensions exist: maximum confidentiality may reduce availability, etc.
key_facts: CIA = Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — the foundational triad
Confidentiality controls: encryption, access control, data classification, DLP
Integrity controls: hashing, digital signatures, checksums, change management
Availability controls: redundancy, load balancing, backups, UPS, DDoS mitigation
Sometimes extended to CIANA (adding Non-repudiation and Authenticity) or Parkerian Hexad
Parkerian Hexad: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability, Possession, Authenticity, Utility
topics.offense_application: Attackers compromise confidentiality (data exfiltration, credential theft), compromise integrity (data tampering, ransomware encryption, DNS poisoning), and compromise availability (DDoS, ransomware, wiping). Each attack type maps to breaking one or more CIA pillars.
topics.defense_application: Defenders classify data by CIA requirements, select controls for each pillar (encryption for C, hashing for I, redundancy for A), and balance all three based on risk. Security frameworks require CIA-based control selection.
drills: For 5 common attacks (phishing, DDoS, ransomware, SQL injection, insider data theft), identify which CIA pillar(s) are compromised
For your organization's top 3 assets, rank CIA priority and justify the ranking
Map each of your existing security controls to which CIA pillar(s) it protects
common_mistakes: Over-focusing on confidentiality and ignoring availability (e.g., over-restrictive encryption that breaks systems)
Confusing data integrity with data accuracy — integrity is about unauthorized modification, not data correctness
Forgetting that backups protect both availability AND integrity (restore unaltered data)

topics.title: Least Privilege, Defense in Depth, and Separation of Duties
concepts: Least Privilege: grant only the minimum access needed to perform a task
Defense in Depth: multiple overlapping security controls (if one fails, others remain)
Separation of Duties (SoD): no single person can complete a sensitive task alone (requires collusion)
Fail Secure: when a system fails, it defaults to a secure state (not open)
Economy of Mechanism: keep security simple to reduce attack surface
Complete Mediation: every access must be checked against the access control system
key_facts: Least privilege is Saltzer and Schroeder's #1 principle (1975)
Defense in depth = layered defense (firewall + IDS + EDR + hardening + monitoring)
Separation of Duties example: one person requests a payment, another approves it
Fail secure example: a firewall failure should block all traffic, not allow all traffic
These principles come from Saltzer & Schroeder 'The Protection of Information in Computer Systems' (1975)
Complete mediation: don't cache access decisions — re-check every time (performance vs security tradeoff)
topics.offense_application: Attackers exploit violations of least privilege (over-privileged service accounts), target single layers when defense in depth is missing, and exploit missing separation of duties (single admin can both create and approve changes).
topics.defense_application: Defenders implement JIT/JEA (Just-In-Time/Just-Enough-Access), design multi-layer security architectures, enforce SoD in business processes (change management, financial controls), and configure systems to fail closed.
drills: Audit a set of user accounts and identify which have more permissions than needed
Design a defense-in-depth architecture for a web application (list all layers and controls)
Identify where SoD violations exist in a sample change management process
common_mistakes: Granting permanent admin access instead of just-in-time elevation — privilege creep
Thinking one layer (e.g., a firewall) is sufficient — defense in depth requires multiple independent layers
Configuring systems to fail open for convenience — should always fail secure/closed

topics.title: Zero Trust Architecture
concepts: Zero Trust: 'Never trust, always verify' — no implicit trust based on network location
Core principle: treat all networks as untrusted, verify every request explicitly
NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture standard
Key pillars: identity, device, network, application, data
Microsegmentation: granular network isolation between applications and workloads
Continuous verification: assess trust dynamically, not just at login
Policy Decision Point (PDP) + Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) architecture
key_facts: Zero Trust replaces 'trust but verify' with 'never trust, always verify'
NIST SP 800-207 (2020) is the authoritative Zero Trust reference
Zero Trust assumes breach — designed to limit blast radius
MFA, conditional access, and microsegmentation are core Zero Trust controls
Traditional perimeter security ('castle and moat') fails once attacker is inside
Zero Trust Maturity Model stages: Traditional → Initial → Advanced → Optimal
Identity-first Zero Trust: starts with strong identity as the primary control plane
topics.offense_application: Attackers exploit traditional perimeter trust models — once they breach the perimeter (phishing, VPN compromise), the flat network gives them free lateral movement. Zero Trust forces them to authenticate at every step.
topics.defense_application: Defenders implement microsegmentation to contain breaches, enforce device compliance and identity verification for every resource access, implement continuous monitoring, and reduce attack surface by removing implicit trust between internal systems.
drills: Compare a traditional 'castle and moat' network to a Zero Trust design — identify where implicit trust exists in the former
Map the 5 Zero Trust pillars (identity, device, network, application, data) to specific controls in your environment
Explain how microsegmentation would have limited the damage of a known breach (e.g., Colonial Pipeline)
common_mistakes: Thinking Zero Trust is a product you buy — it's an architecture and mindset requiring organizational change
Believing Zero Trust eliminates all network controls — network controls still matter, they're just not the only control
Implementing Zero Trust only for remote access — it applies to internal traffic too

modules.title: Risk Management and Threat Modeling
modules.objective: Assess security risk using structured frameworks and apply threat modeling methodologies (STRIDE, PASTA, DREAD) to systems.

topics.title: Risk Assessment Fundamentals
concepts: Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact (or Likelihood × Impact)
Asset: anything of value (data, systems, reputation)
Threat: potential cause of unwanted incident (adversary, natural disaster)
Vulnerability: weakness that a threat can exploit
Impact: consequence if the risk materializes
Risk treatment options: Accept, Mitigate (reduce), Transfer (insurance), Avoid
Residual risk: remaining risk after controls are applied
Qualitative vs quantitative risk analysis
key_facts: Risk formula: Risk = Likelihood × Impact (commonly used)
ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) = SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) × ARO (Annual Rate of Occurrence)
SLE = Asset Value × Exposure Factor
Risk matrix typically uses 5x5 or 3x3 Likelihood × Impact grid
Risk appetite: amount of risk an organization is willing to accept
Risk tolerance: acceptable variation around risk appetite
topics.offense_application: Attackers perform their own risk assessment — targeting high-value assets with exploitable vulnerabilities and high impact. They prioritize attacks with highest ROI (effort vs reward).
topics.defense_application: Defenders use risk assessment to prioritize security investments, justify budgets, focus remediation on highest-risk vulnerabilities (not just CVSS scores), and communicate risk to leadership in business terms.
drills: Build a 5x5 risk matrix and place 10 threats on it (likelihood × impact)
Calculate ALE for a scenario: asset worth $500K, exposure factor 40%, occurs 3x/year
For your top 5 risks, assign a treatment (accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid) and justify
common_mistakes: Equating risk with vulnerability — risk also depends on threat and impact
Focusing only on technical risk while ignoring business and reputational risk
Treating risk assessment as a one-time activity — it must be continuous and updated

topics.title: Threat Modeling — STRIDE
concepts: STRIDE: Microsoft's threat categorization mnemonic
S = Spoofing (impersonating identity)
T = Tampering (modifying data)
R = Repudiation (denying an action)
I = Information Disclosure (data exposure)
D = Denial of Service (availability disruption)
E = Elevation of Privilege (gaining unauthorized access levels)
STRIDE maps to CIA+ (each letter corresponds to a security property)
key_facts: STRIDE was developed by Microsoft (Loren Kohnfelder and Praerit Garg, 1999)
Spoofing → breaks Authentication
Tampering → breaks Integrity
Repudiation → breaks Non-repudiation
Information Disclosure → breaks Confidentiality
Denial of Service → breaks Availability
Elevation of Privilege → breaks Authorization
STRIDE-per-element: apply STRIDE to each element in a data flow diagram (DFD)
topics.offense_application: Attackers intuitively map their attacks to STRIDE categories — phishing is Spoofing, data breach is Information Disclosure, ransomware is Tampering + DoS, privilege escalation is Elevation of Privilege.
topics.defense_application: Defenders use STRIDE during design phase to systematically identify threats, create a data flow diagram (DFD), apply STRIDE to each element/flow/data store, and design controls for each identified threat. This is proactive security.
drills: Create a DFD for a simple web application and apply STRIDE to each element
Map 10 common attacks to STRIDE categories
Design a control for each STRIDE category applied to an authentication system
common_mistakes: Starting STRIDE without a data flow diagram — the DFD is essential context
Only applying STRIDE to external-facing components — internal components have threats too
Using STRIDE only once — it should be applied during design AND when architecture changes

topics.title: PASTA, DREAD, and Security Frameworks (NIST CSF, ISO 27001)
concepts: PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis): 7-stage risk-centric threat modeling
DREAD: risk rating model — Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected Users, Discoverability
NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF): Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover (+ Govern in 2.0)
ISO 27001: international standard for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS)
ISO 27002: controls and best practices complementing ISO 27001
CIS Controls: prioritized set of best practices (18 control areas)
MITRE ATT&CK: knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques
key_facts: PASTA stages: 1) Define objectives, 2) Define technical scope, 3) Application decomposition, 4) Threat analysis, 5) Vulnerability analysis, 6) Attack modeling, 7) Risk analysis
DREAD score: average of D+R+E+A+D (each 1-10), higher = higher risk
NIST CSF 2.0 (2024) added 'Govern' as a sixth function: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover, Govern
NIST CSF profiles: Core, Tiers (1-4), Profiles
ISO 27001 requires: risk assessment, risk treatment plan, Statement of Applicability (SoA), ISMS
ISO 27001 certification requires audit by accredited body
CIS Controls v8 has 18 control areas with 153 safeguards (IG1/IG2/IG3 tiers)
MITRE ATT&CK organizes by Tactics (the 'why') and Techniques (the 'how')
topics.offense_application: Attackers are mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques by defenders; threat models like PASTA simulate realistic attack chains. Understanding frameworks helps predict where attackers focus.
topics.defense_application: Defenders use NIST CSF as a security program roadmap, ISO 27001 for certification and compliance, CIS Controls for prioritized hardening, MITRE ATT&CK for detection engineering, and PASTA for deep threat modeling.
drills: Rate 3 vulnerabilities using DREAD and compare scores to CVSS
Map your current security program to the 6 NIST CSF 2.0 functions — identify gaps
Walk through PASTA's 7 stages for a specific application in your environment
common_mistakes: Confusing ISO 27001 (the standard/certification) with ISO 27002 (the controls guidance)
Treating frameworks as checklists rather than continuous improvement programs
Using DREAD alone without context — it's a quick rating, not a comprehensive risk analysis

modules.title: Compliance and Governance
modules.objective: Explain major regulatory frameworks (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, SOC 2, FedRAMP) and how they drive security requirements.

topics.title: GDPR and Data Privacy Regulations
concepts: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): EU data protection law (enforced May 2018)
Applies to any organization processing EU residents' personal data, regardless of location
Key principles: lawfulness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality
Data subject rights: access, rectification, erasure ('right to be forgotten'), portability, objection
Data Protection Officer (DPO): required for certain organizations
Data breach notification: 72 hours to supervisory authority
Lawful basis for processing: consent, contract, legal obligation, legitimate interest, etc.
key_facts: GDPR went into effect May 25, 2018
Maximum fine: €20 million or 4% of global annual revenue, whichever is higher
Data breach notification deadline: 72 hours from awareness
Personal data: any information relating to an identified or identifiable person
Special category data: health, biometric, genetic, racial/ethnic, religious, political, sexual orientation — stricter rules
CCPA/CPRA: California's equivalent data privacy law
Other privacy laws: LGPD (Brazil), PIPEDA (Canada), UK DPA
topics.offense_application: Data breaches trigger GDPR notification requirements (72-hour deadline). Attackers target personal data for identity theft, ransom, or sale. The regulatory consequences make data breaches costly beyond technical remediation.
topics.defense_application: Defenders implement data classification and DLP to identify and protect personal data, maintain data inventory, enforce encryption at rest/in transit, implement data retention policies, and have incident response procedures aligned with 72-hour notification requirements.
drills: Map an organization's data flows and identify where personal data is stored, processed, and transmitted
Draft a GDPR-compliant data breach notification template including required elements
Identify which data in a sample database constitutes 'special category data' under GDPR
common_mistakes: Thinking GDPR only applies to EU companies — it applies to ANY organization processing EU residents' data
Ignoring data subject rights requests — must respond within 1 month
Storing unnecessary personal data — GDPR requires data minimization

topics.title: HIPAA and PCI-DSS
concepts: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act): US healthcare data protection (1996)
HIPAA Rules: Privacy Rule, Security Rule, Breach Notification Rule
Protected Health Information (PHI): individually identifiable health information
PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard): credit card data protection
PCI-DSS requirements: 12 requirements across 6 control objectives
PCI scope: cardholder data environment (CDE) — everything that touches card data
PCI-DSS 4.0 (current version, mandatory March 2024+)
key_facts: HIPAA applies to covered entities (healthcare providers, plans, clearinghouses) and business associates
PHI examples: medical records, insurance information, SSN + health data
HIPAA Security Rule has administrative, physical, and technical safeguards

PCI-DSS v4.0 has 12 requirements including: firewalls, no default passwords, protect stored cardholder data, encrypt transmission, maintain AV, develop secure systems, restrict access, track/monitor access, test security, maintain an information security policy
PCI levels based on transaction volume: Level 1 (>6M transactions/year) requires formal audit
PCI scope reduction: tokenization and network segmentation reduce audit scope
Cardholder data: PAN (Primary Account Number), cardholder name, expiration date, service code
PCI prohibits storing CVV/CVC after authorization
topics.offense_application: Attackers target healthcare (ransomware on hospitals — high impact, HIPAA violations), payment card data (credit card skimming, Magecart attacks, POS malware). Stolen PHI sells for more than credit cards on dark web.
topics.defense_application: Defenders reduce PCI scope via tokenization and segmentation, encrypt all PHI and cardholder data, implement access controls and audit logging, conduct regular penetration tests, and maintain compliance documentation.
drills: Design a network architecture that isolates the cardholder data environment (CDE) from the rest of the network
Identify which PCI-DSS requirements address encryption, access control, and monitoring
Given a hospital data breach scenario, identify which HIPAA rules were violated
common_mistakes: Storing CVV/CVC codes — PCI-DSS explicitly prohibits post-authorization storage
Underestimating PCI scope — any system that can impact CDE security is in scope
Thinking HIPAA is only about IT — it covers administrative and physical safeguards too

topics.title: SOC 2 and FedRAMP
concepts: SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2): AICPA framework for service organization security
SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria (TSC): Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy
SOC 2 Type I: point-in-time design assessment; Type II: effectiveness over a period (6-12 months)
FedRAMP (Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program): US government cloud security authorization
FedRAMP levels: Low, Moderate, High impact
FedRAMP authorization: requires 3PAO (Third-Party Assessment Organization) assessment
FISMA: Federal Information Security Modernization Act — broader federal security requirement
key_facts: SOC 2 Type I = design suitability at a point in time; Type II = operating effectiveness over 6-12 months
SOC 2 Security criterion is required; others (Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy) are optional add-ons
SOC 1 (SSAE 18) = financial controls; SOC 2 = security controls; SOC 3 = public summary of SOC 2
FedRAMP Moderate is the most common authorization level — protects non-public CUI
FedRAMP High = high-impact data (life-threatening, major financial loss if breached)
FedRAMP requires continuous monitoring (ConMon) after authorization
ATO (Authority to Operate): final authorization from the agency
StateRAMP: state/local government equivalent of FedRAMP
topics.offense_application: Attackers target SOC 2/FedRAMP-certified organizations knowing they hold sensitive data. Compliance certifications don't guarantee security — gaps between audited controls and actual practice create exploitable weaknesses.
topics.defense_application: Defenders use SOC 2/FedRAMP requirements as comprehensive security program baselines, implement continuous monitoring, maintain evidence for audits, and use compliance requirements to justify security investments.
drills: Compare SOC 2 Type I vs Type II reports and explain why Type II is more valuable
Map the 5 SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria to specific security controls
Explain the FedRAMP authorization process from preparation to ATO
common_mistakes: Treating SOC 2 as a one-time certification — it requires annual Type II audits
Confusing SOC 1 (financial controls) with SOC 2 (security controls)
Thinking compliance = security — compliance is a minimum baseline, not comprehensive protection

modules.title: Web Security Fundamentals
modules.objective: Explain HTTP mechanics, web session management, REST APIs, and browser security policies including CORS and same-origin policy.

topics.title: HTTP Methods and Status Codes
concepts: HTTP methods: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove)
Safe methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — should not modify server state
Idempotent methods: GET, PUT, DELETE — same result no matter how many times called
Status codes: 1xx (informational), 2xx (success), 3xx (redirect), 4xx (client error), 5xx (server error)
Common status codes: 200 (OK), 301/302 (redirect), 304 (Not Modified), 400 (Bad Request), 401 (Unauthorized), 403 (Forbidden), 404 (Not Found), 500 (Internal Server Error), 503 (Service Unavailable)
key_facts: GET requests can be cached/bookmarked; POST requests cannot
401 Unauthorized = not authenticated (no/invalid credentials)
403 Forbidden = authenticated but not authorized (insufficient permissions)
500 = server-side error (may leak stack traces/info)
PUT is idempotent (calling twice = same result); POST is not (calling twice creates two resources)
OPTIONS method used for CORS preflight requests
TRACE method = XSS risk (XST - Cross-Site Tracing), should be disabled
Idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS; NOT idempotent: POST, PATCH (debated)
topics.offense_application: Attackers manipulate HTTP methods for exploitation: parameter tampering in GET/POST, method override to access restricted functionality, verbose error responses (500) for information gathering, and forced browsing.
topics.defense_application: Defenders restrict allowed HTTP methods on web servers, return generic error pages (no stack traces), implement proper status code usage (401 vs 403 distinction), and monitor for unusual method usage.
drills: Use curl to make requests with different HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) against a test API
Examine server error responses and identify information leakage in 500 errors
Explain the security implications of each common status code
common_mistakes: Using GET for actions that modify state (violates HTTP spec, vulnerable to CSRF via image tags/links)
Confusing 401 (unauthenticated) with 403 (unauthorized) — return 401 when login is needed, 403 when permissions are insufficient
Returning detailed error messages (stack traces, SQL queries) in 500 responses — information disclosure

topics.title: Cookies and Session Management
concepts: Cookie: key-value pair sent by server, stored by browser, sent with subsequent requests
Session management: server maintains state across stateless HTTP using session IDs (in cookies)
Cookie attributes: HttpOnly (no JS access), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite (cross-site policy), Domain, Path, Max-Age/Expires
