SameSite values: Strict (no cross-site), Lax (top-level GET navigation only), None (requires Secure)
JWT as stateless session tokens vs server-side sessions
Session fixation: attacker sets a known session ID, victim authenticates with it
key_facts: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading cookies (mitigates session theft via XSS)
Secure ensures cookies only sent over HTTPS
SameSite=Strict: cookie not sent on cross-site requests at all
SameSite=Lax (browser default since 2020): sent on top-level navigation (GET) only
SameSite=None: sent cross-site but REQUIRES Secure attribute
Session ID should be: long, random, unpredictable, regenerated after login
Common cookie-based attacks: session hijacking (steal cookie), CSRF (force authenticated request), session fixation
topics.offense_application: Attackers steal cookies via XSS (if no HttpOnly), intercept them via MITM (if no Secure), perform CSRF (if no SameSite), and use session fixation to hijack sessions. Cookie theft bypasses MFA since the session is already authenticated.
topics.defense_application: Defenders set HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite on all session cookies, regenerate session IDs after login, set short session timeouts, implement CSRF tokens, and use HSTS to prevent cookie interception.
drills: Inspect cookies in browser DevTools and evaluate each attribute (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite)
Explain how HttpOnly prevents session theft via document.cookie in XSS
Demonstrate CSRF and explain how SameSite=Lax and CSRF tokens mitigate it
common_mistakes: Forgetting to set HttpOnly — allows XSS to steal session cookies
Setting SameSite=None without Secure — browser rejects it
Not regenerating session ID after login — enables session fixation

topics.title: Same-Origin Policy and CORS
concepts: Same-Origin Policy (SOP): browser security model — scripts can only access resources from the same origin
Origin = scheme (protocol) + host (domain) + port — all three must match
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): mechanism to relax SOP for specific cross-origin requests
CORS preflight: browser sends OPTIONS request before certain cross-origin requests
CORS headers: Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is dangerous when combined with Allow-Credentials: true (browsers block this)
key_facts: Same-origin = same protocol + same host + same port (e.g., https://a.com:443 ≠ http://a.com:80)
SOP prevents malicious.com from reading data from bank.com via JavaScript
CORS is a server-side mechanism — the server decides which origins can access its resources
Preflight (OPTIONS) required for: non-simple methods (PUT, DELETE), custom headers, non-simple content types
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * allows any origin but CANNOT be used with credentials
Reflecting Origin header in Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Allow-Credentials: true is a critical CORS vulnerability
CORS does NOT protect against CSRF — CSRF doesn't need to read the response
topics.offense_application: Attackers exploit misconfigured CORS: wildcard origins with credentials, Origin header reflection, null origin handling, to read cross-origin responses from authenticated sessions. SOP bypasses enable data theft.
topics.defense_application: Defenders configure CORS with explicit allowlists (not wildcards), never reflect Origin headers, validate origin against a server-side allowlist, and understand that CORS is not a substitute for authentication/authorization.
drills: Identify the origin of three URLs and determine if they are same-origin with each other
Examine a CORS response in browser DevTools — identify misconfigured headers
Explain why Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with Allow-Credentials: true is blocked by browsers
common_mistakes: Thinking CORS is a security feature that protects you — it RELAXES security, configure carefully
Using Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * for authenticated APIs — allows any site to read responses (but not with credentials)
Confusing SOP with CORS — SOP is the browser's restriction; CORS is the exception mechanism

topics.title: REST APIs and API Security
concepts: REST (Representational State Transfer): architectural style for web APIs
REST principles: statelessness, client-server, cacheable, uniform interface, layered
Resources identified by URLs: /api/users/123, /api/orders/456
Standard methods map to CRUD: GET (Read), POST (Create), PUT (Update), DELETE (Delete)
API authentication: API keys, OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens, JWT, mutual TLS
API security concerns: broken object level authorization (BOLA/IDOR), excessive data exposure, rate limiting
key_facts: REST is stateless — each request contains all needed information, no server-side session
Common API security risks from OWASP API Top 10: BOLA, broken authentication, excessive data exposure, lack of rate limiting, broken function level authorization
BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) / IDOR: accessing other users' data by changing object IDs in URLs
API versioning: /api/v1/users vs /api/v2/users
Rate limiting prevents brute force and DoS — typically measured in requests per minute
GraphQL APIs have different security concerns: introspection, query depth/complexity attacks
HTTP status codes in REST APIs: 200 (success), 201 (created), 204 (no content), 400 (bad request), 401 (unauthenticated), 403 (forbidden), 404 (not found), 429 (rate limited)
topics.offense_application: Attackers exploit API vulnerabilities: BOLA to access other users' data, enumerate IDs, abuse lack of rate limiting for brute force, extract excessive data from responses, and abuse broken authentication.
topics.defense_application: Defenders implement object-level authorization checks on every request, enforce rate limiting, minimize data in responses (no sensitive fields by default), validate input, and use API gateways with security controls.
drills: Identify BOLA/IDOR vulnerabilities by manipulating object IDs in API requests
Design a REST API with proper CRUD operations and identify where authorization checks are needed
Implement and test rate limiting on an API endpoint
common_mistakes: Relying on client-side authorization (hidden buttons/menus) — server must enforce authorization on every request
Not implementing rate limiting on API endpoints — enables brute force and data harvesting
Returning entire database records instead of only needed fields — excessive data exposure

modules.title: Cloud and Containerization Fundamentals
modules.objective: Explain cloud service models, the shared responsibility model, and containerization basics (Docker/Kubernetes).

topics.title: Cloud Service Models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and Shared Responsibility
concepts: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): VMs, storage, networking (AWS EC2, Azure VM, GCP Compute Engine)
PaaS (Platform as a Service): managed runtime, databases, app hosting (Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk)
SaaS (Software as a Service): ready-to-use applications (Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Google Workspace)
FaaS (Functions as a Service): serverless computing (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions)
Shared Responsibility Model: cloud provider vs customer security responsibilities differ by service model
On-premises: customer responsible for everything
IaaS: provider secures infrastructure; customer secures OS, apps, data
SaaS: provider secures most; customer secures data and access
key_facts: IaaS customer responsibilities: OS patching, application security, data, identity/access, network config
SaaS customer responsibilities: data, access management, configuration, compliance
PaaS falls between IaaS and SaaS — provider manages OS and runtime
Misconfiguration is the #1 cloud security risk (human error, not provider failure)
Cloud provider NEVER takes responsibility for: your data, your access (IAM), your compliance
Common cloud misconfigurations: public S3 buckets, overly permissive IAM roles, exposed security groups, default credentials
Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM): tools to detect cloud misconfigurations
topics.offense_application: Attackers exploit cloud misconfigurations: public storage buckets (open S3), overly permissive IAM, exposed management interfaces, leaked cloud credentials in code/GitHub, and unencrypted data stores.
topics.defense_application: Defenders implement least-privilege IAM, enable cloud logging (CloudTrail, Activity Log), use CSPM tools, encrypt all data, enable MFA on all cloud accounts, and conduct regular configuration audits.
drills: Map the shared responsibility model for IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — identify what you're responsible for in each
Audit an AWS/Azure account for common misconfigurations (public buckets, IAM policies, security groups)
Identify cloud credentials that might be accidentally leaked in code repositories
common_mistakes: Assuming the cloud provider secures everything — shared responsibility means YOU own significant security
Leaving storage buckets public by default — one of the most common and damaging misconfigurations
Using root/admin cloud accounts for day-to-day operations — use IAM roles with least privilege

topics.title: Containerization with Docker
concepts: Container: lightweight, portable, self-contained application + dependencies package
Docker image: read-only template with instructions for creating a container (layers)
Dockerfile: text file of instructions to build an image (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD, etc.)
Container vs VM: containers share the host OS kernel; VMs have full guest OS
Docker daemon: background service managing containers, images, volumes, networks
Docker registry: stores and distributes images (Docker Hub, private registries, ECR/ACR/GCR)
Container orchestration: Docker Swarm (simpler), Kubernetes (industry standard)
key_facts: Containers share the host kernel — isolated via namespaces and cgroups, not full virtualization
Namespaces isolate: PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user
cgroups limit: CPU, memory, disk I/O, network bandwidth
By default, containers run as root (UID 0) — security risk
Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) = root access to host — never expose it
Common security issues: running as root, no resource limits, exposed Docker daemon (port 2375 unencrypted), vulnerable base images, no image scanning
Image scanning tools: Trivy, Clair, Snyk, Aqua — detect vulnerabilities in image layers
Distroless images: contain only application runtime, no shell/package manager — smaller attack surface
topics.offense_application: Attackers exploit containers: container escape to host (run as root + privileged), compromise vulnerable images, access exposed Docker daemon API (port 2375/2376), poison images in registry (supply chain), and mine cryptocurrency using container resources.
topics.defense_application: Defenders run containers as non-root user, use read-only filesystems, enable seccomp/AppArmor profiles, scan images for vulnerabilities, use distroless/minimal base images, never expose Docker daemon without TLS/auth, and use private registries with image signing.
drills: Write a Dockerfile that follows security best practices (non-root user, minimal base, no secrets)
Scan a Docker image with Trivy and identify vulnerabilities
Explain how a container escape works when running in privileged mode
common_mistakes: Running containers as root — the default but most dangerous configuration
Using --privileged flag — gives container near-host-level access, almost always unnecessary
Not scanning images — vulnerable base images propagate CVEs into production

topics.title: Kubernetes Fundamentals
concepts: Kubernetes (K8s): container orchestration platform for deploying, scaling, and managing containers
Cluster architecture: control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) + worker nodes
Core objects: Pod (smallest deployable unit), Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Namespace
etcd: distributed key-value store holding all cluster state — critical to secure
K8s API server: central management API (usually port 6443, HTTPS) — all operations go through it
RBAC: Role-Based Access Control for K8s API — Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoleBindings
Pod security: security contexts, Pod Security Standards (privileged, baseline, restricted)
key_facts: K8s API server listens on port 6443 (HTTPS) or 8080 (insecure, deprecated, should be disabled)
etcd stores ALL cluster data including Secrets — must be encrypted at rest
kubelet port: 10250 (HTTPS), 10255 (read-only HTTP, should be disabled)
K8s Secrets: base64-encoded (NOT encrypted by default) — enable encryption at rest
ServiceAccount tokens: auto-mounted into pods by default — can be abused for cluster API access
Common K8s attacks: exposed API server, etcd without auth, RBAC misconfiguration, container escape, compromised ServiceAccount token
K8s network policies: restrict pod-to-pod communication (default: all pods can communicate)
Tools: kubectl (CLI), Helm (package manager), kube-bench (CIS benchmark), kube-hunter (pentest)
topics.offense_application: Attackers exploit exposed K8s API servers, steal ServiceAccount tokens from compromised pods, access unencrypted etcd for Secrets, exploit RBAC misconfigurations for privilege escalation, and perform container escapes to node access.
topics.defense_application: Defenders secure the API server (RBAC, network policies, audit logging), encrypt etcd at rest, restrict pod-to-pod communication with network policies, use Pod Security Standards (restricted), disable auto-mounted ServiceAccount tokens, and scan with kube-bench.
drills: Use kubectl to enumerate cluster resources and identify potential misconfigurations
Explain why K8s Secrets being base64-encoded is NOT encryption
Design network policies to restrict pod-to-pod communication to only necessary connections
common_mistakes: Believing K8s Secrets are encrypted — they are only base64-encoded by default, enable encryption at rest
Leaving the API server exposed without authentication — catastrophic
Using default ServiceAccount tokens that auto-mount into every pod — abuse vector for cluster access

modules.title: Scripting and Automation for Security
modules.objective: Use Bash, PowerShell, and Python for common security tasks including reconnaissance, log analysis, and automation.

topics.title: Bash Scripting for Security
concepts: Bash: default shell on most Linux systems, powerful scripting language
Variables: VAR=value, $VAR, ${VAR}, command substitution $(command)
Pipes and redirects: | (pipe), > (redirect output), >> (append), < (input)
Text processing: grep (search), awk (column processing), sed (stream editing), cut, sort, uniq
Conditionals: if/elif/else, test [ ], case statements
Loops: for, while, until
Security-focused one-liners: log parsing, network scanning, file enumeration
key_facts: Shebang: #!/bin/bash (first line of script)
grep -r: recursive search, -i: case-insensitive, -E: extended regex
awk '{print $1}': print first column, -F',' sets delimiter
sed 's/old/new/g': global substitution
sort | uniq -c | sort -rn: count and sort occurrences (frequency analysis)
Common security commands: find / -perm -4000 (SUID), ps aux (processes), netstat -tulpn (listening ports), ss -tulpn (modern replacement)
xargs: build and execute commands from standard input
Bash scripts should start with set -euo pipefail (fail fast on errors)
topics.offense_application: Attackers use Bash for enumeration and automation: finding SUID binaries, searching for passwords in config files, pivoting through systems, parsing /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow, and automating exploitation.
topics.defense_application: Defenders use Bash for log analysis (grep auth.log for failed logins), system auditing (find world-writable files), incident response triage, and automating security checks across many systems.
drills: Write a script to find all SUID/SGID binaries and output to a file
Parse auth.log to count failed SSH login attempts per IP address
Create a script that enumerates open ports, running processes, and scheduled tasks
common_mistakes: Not quoting variables — unquoted $VAR with spaces causes word splitting and globbing
Using eval carelessly — can lead to command injection in scripts
Not using set -euo pipefail — scripts continue after errors, masking failures

topics.title: PowerShell for Security
concepts: PowerShell: Windows task automation and configuration management framework (.NET-based)
Cmdlets: Verb-Noun naming (Get-Process, Set-Item, Invoke-WebRequest)
Pipeline: output objects (not text) between cmdlets
Aliases: ls → Get-ChildItem, cat → Get-Content, curl → Invoke-WebRequest
Security-relevant modules: ActiveDirectory, NetTCPIP, Defender, EventLog
PowerShell remoting: Enter-PSSession, Invoke-Command — remote management
Execution Policy: controls script execution (Restricted, RemoteSigned, Unrestricted)
key_facts: PowerShell cmdlet naming: Verb-Noun (e.g., Get-ADUser, Set-ExecutionPolicy)
Get-Help <cmdlet>: documentation; Get-Command: find cmdlets; Get-Member: inspect object properties
Execution Policy can be bypassed: -ExecutionPolicy Bypass flag
PowerShell version 5+ has enhanced logging (ScriptBlock logging, Transcription)
Common security cmdlets: Get-EventLog/Get-WinEvent, Get-Process, Get-Service, Get-NetTCPConnection, Get-LocalUser
AMSI (Anti-Malware Scan Interface): scans PowerShell scripts before execution
Invoke-Mimikatz, PowerSploit, PowerView: offensive PowerShell frameworks
PowerShell Core (7.x) is cross-platform (.NET Core); Windows PowerShell (5.1) is Windows-only
topics.offense_application: Attackers use PowerShell extensively: living-off-the-land (blend with admin activity), memory injection, credential dumping (Mimikatz via PowerShell), lateral movement (Invoke-Command), and downloading/executing payloads (Invoke-WebRequest + Invoke-Expression).
topics.defense_application: Defenders enable PowerShell logging (ScriptBlock logging Event ID 4104, Module logging, Transcription), use Constrained Language Mode, deploy AMSI, monitor for suspicious patterns (encoded commands, Invoke-Expression, downloads), and use PowerShell for incident response.
drills: Write a PowerShell script to enumerate all running processes and their network connections
Query Windows Event Logs for all failed logon attempts in the last 24 hours
Analyze a malicious PowerShell one-liner — decode base64, identify the payload, and explain AMSI's role
common_mistakes: Disabling PowerShell entirely 'for security' — it removes a critical defender tool; secure it with logging instead
Forgetting that Execution Policy is not a security boundary — trivially bypassed
Ignoring PowerShell ScriptBlock logging — it's the most valuable detection source for malicious PowerShell

topics.title: Python for Security
concepts: Python: versatile language widely used in security tools and automation
Key libraries: socket (networking), requests (HTTP), scapy (packet manipulation), paramiko (SSH)
Security tooling libraries: hashlib, cryptography, ssl, subprocess
Offensive libraries: pwntools (exploit dev), requests/scapy (recon), pycryptodome (crypto)
Defensive libraries: psutil (process monitoring), dpkt/pyshark (pcap analysis), yara-python (malware signatures)
Python scripts for: port scanning, log analysis, password cracking, exploit development, malware analysis
key_facts: Python 3 is the standard (Python 2 EOL was January 2020)
socket library: raw TCP/UDP networking — socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)
requests library: simplified HTTP — requests.get(), requests.post()
scapy: packet crafting/sniffing — can forge, decode, send, capture packets
Python is the primary language for: exploit development, security tooling, automation scripts, ML/AI security
virtualenv / pip: package management for isolated environments
Common security tools written in Python: Scapy, Nmap (has Python bindings), Volatility (memory forensics), sqlmap
topics.offense_application: Attackers use Python for custom exploit development, automation of reconnaissance, writing C2 implants, packet sniffing/injection (scapy), and rapid prototyping of attack tools.
topics.defense_application: Defenders use Python for log analysis at scale, automating incident response, building detection rules, network traffic analysis, malware analysis (Volatility framework), and security tooling integration.
drills: Write a Python port scanner using the socket library
Use scapy to capture and analyze DNS queries on your network
Write a script to parse a web server access log and identify potential SQL injection attempts
common_mistakes: Using Python 2 syntax (print without parentheses) — Python 3 is required
Not handling socket timeouts in network scripts — can hang indefinitely
Using subprocess with shell=True and unsanitized input — command injection vulnerability

modules.title: Malware Fundamentals
modules.objective: Classify malware types, explain propagation and persistence mechanisms, and compare static vs dynamic analysis approaches.

topics.title: Types of Malware
concepts: Virus: self-replicating code that attaches to host files, requires user execution to spread
Worm: self-replicating malware that spreads automatically across networks without user action
Trojan: disguised as legitimate software, creates backdoor access
Ransomware: encrypts victim's data and demands payment for decryption key
Rootkit: maintains persistent privileged access while hiding its presence
Spyware: covertly collects user information and activity
Botnet: network of compromised machines controlled by a central C2 (zombie/bot)
Adware: displays unwanted advertisements, may collect data
Wiper: destroys data irreversibly (intent is destruction, not extortion)
Cryptominer: hijacks system resources to mine cryptocurrency
Logic bomb: executes malicious action when triggered by specific condition/date
key_facts: Virus requires a host file and user action; Worm spreads autonomously over networks
Ransomware variants: crypto (encrypts files), locker (locks screen/system), double-extortion (encrypt + threaten to leak)
Notable ransomware: WannaCry (2017, EternalBlue exploit), NotPetya (2017, wiper disguised as ransomware), Ryuk, Conti, LockBit
Rootkit types: user-mode (ring 3), kernel-mode (ring 0), bootkit (MBR/UEFI), firmware/hardware
Botnet C2 architectures: centralized (IRC, HTTP) vs decentralized (P2P)
Polymorphic malware: changes its code signature each infection to evade AV
Metamorphic malware: rewrites its own code completely each infection
Fileless malware: resides in memory (RAM) only — no files on disk, evades traditional AV
topics.offense_application: Attackers deploy specific malware types for their objectives: ransomware for extortion, worms for rapid spread (WannaCry), rootkits for persistent stealth, fileless malware to evade AV, and cryptominers for passive income.
topics.defense_application: Defenders deploy EDR/AV (signature + behavior-based), implement application whitelisting, use network segmentation to contain worm propagation, maintain offline backups against ransomware, and hunt for fileless malware in memory.
drills: Create a malware classification chart: given 10 malware samples, categorize each type
Research WannaCry and trace its propagation method (EternalBlue, SMB port 445)
Explain the difference between polymorphic and metamorphic malware evasion
common_mistakes: Confusing virus (needs host + user action) with worm (self-propagating)
Thinking AV signatures catch all malware — polymorphic, metamorphic, and fileless malware evade signatures
Believing paying ransomware ransom guarantees data recovery — no guarantee, and funds future attacks

topics.title: Malware Analysis Approaches
concepts: Static analysis: examining malware without executing it
Dynamic analysis: executing malware in a controlled environment and observing behavior
Static techniques: file hashing, string extraction, disassembly (IDA, Ghidra), PE header analysis, unpacking
Dynamic techniques: sandbox execution, API call monitoring, network traffic capture, memory dump analysis
Hybrid analysis: combining static and dynamic for comprehensive understanding
Reverse engineering: disassembly/decompilation to understand malware logic and capabilities
Malware analysis environments: isolated VMs, sandboxes (Cuckoo, Any.Run), FLARE-VM
key_facts: Static analysis first step: hash the file (SHA-256) and check against VirusTotal
String extraction (strings command) reveals URLs, API names, error messages, embedded text
PE header analysis: imports (IAT), sections, compile timestamp, entropy (packed sections have high entropy)
Packing: malware compressed/encrypted to evade static analysis — must unpack first
Common packers: UPX, Themida, VMProtect, custom packers
Dynamic analysis tools: Process Monitor, Process Explorer, Wireshark, API Monitor, FakeNet
Sandbox tools: Cuckoo Sandbox, Any.Run, Joe Sandbox, FireEye AX
Disassemblers/Decompilers: IDA Pro, Ghidra (free, NSA), Radare2, Binary Ninja
Indicators of Compromise (IOCs): file hashes, IP addresses, domains, mutex names, registry keys
topics.offense_application: Malware authors evade analysis: packing/encryption (anti-static), sandbox detection and anti-debugging (anti-dynamic), timing delays, environment checks (VM detection, debuggers), and obfuscated code.
topics.defense_application: Defenders analyze malware to extract IOCs for detection, understand capabilities for incident response, develop signatures/YARA rules, attribute to threat actors, and assess the scope and impact of an infection.
drills: Run 'strings' on a malware sample and identify indicators (URLs, IPs, API calls)
Submit a malware hash to VirusTotal and analyze the detection results
Set up a Cuckoo sandbox or use Any.Run to perform dynamic analysis on a sample — document observed behaviors
common_mistakes: Executing malware on a production/host machine — always use isolated VMs with snapshots
Relying only on static OR dynamic analysis — both are needed for complete understanding
Forgetting to check if malware is packed — static analysis of packed malware reveals nothing useful

topics.title: Malware Lifecycle, Persistence, and IOCs
concepts: Malware kill chain: delivery, execution, persistence, C2, lateral movement, actions on objectives
Persistence mechanisms: registry Run keys, scheduled tasks, services, startup folders, WMI, DLL hijacking
C2 (Command and Control): communication channel for attacker to send commands to compromised host
Common C2 protocols: HTTP(S), DNS tunneling, ICMP, custom protocols
Indicators of Compromise (IOCs): artifacts that indicate a system was compromised
IOC types: file hashes, file names, registry keys, mutexes, network indicators (IPs, domains, URLs), behavioral patterns
MITRE ATT&CK mapping: relate observed malware behaviors to known tactics and techniques
Threat intelligence: sharing IOCs and analysis across organizations (MISP, STIX/TAXII)
key_facts: Mutex names are reliable IOCs — malware creates named mutexes to prevent multiple infections
Common C2 frameworks: Cobalt Strike (commercial/leaked), Metasploit, Sliver, Mythic, Brute Ratel
Beaconing: C2 traffic with regular intervals (jitter makes detection harder)
YARA rules: pattern-matching tool for identifying malware by textual/binary patterns
STIX (Structured Threat Information Expression) and TAXII (Trusted Automated Exchange) are IOC sharing standards
Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis: adversary, infrastructure, capability, victim
Pyramid of Pain: hash > IP > domain > network artifact > host artifact > tools > TTPs — higher = more painful for attacker to change
topics.offense_application: Attackers establish persistence through multiple independent mechanisms (if one is found, others remain), use stealthy C2 with jitter and legitimate-looking protocols, and employ living-off-the-land techniques to blend with normal activity.
topics.defense_application: Defenders hunt for IOCs across endpoints and networks, map detections to MITRE ATT&CK, implement threat intelligence feeds, detect C2 beaconing patterns, use YARA for file scanning, and share IOCs via MISP/STIX for community defense.
drills: Given a set of IOCs from an incident, categorize each by type (file, network, host, behavioral) and map to MITRE ATT&CK techniques
Write a simple YARA rule to detect a known malware string pattern
Explain the Pyramid of Pain and why detecting TTPs is more valuable than detecting IP addresses
common_mistakes: Removing malware without finding ALL persistence mechanisms — it returns after reboot
Blocking a C2 IP without understanding the full infrastructure — attackers rotate IPs quickly
Focusing on file hashes as IOCs — trivially changed by attackers; TTPs are more durable

modules.title: Social Engineering Fundamentals
modules.objective: Identify social engineering attack types including phishing, pretexting, and business email compromise, and explain human-layer defenses.

topics.title: Phishing and Variants
concepts: Phishing: fraudulent communications impersonating a trusted entity to steal credentials/data
Spear phishing: targeted phishing aimed at specific individuals (personalized, researched)
Whaling: phishing targeting high-profile individuals (executives, C-suite)
Smishing: phishing via SMS/text messages
Vishing: phishing via voice/phone calls
Clone phishing: duplicating a legitimate email and replacing links/attachments with malicious ones
Phishing kits: pre-built packages for creating phishing pages (often sold on dark web)
Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM): reverse proxy that intercepts credentials AND MFA tokens
key_facts: Phishing is the #1 initial access vector in breaches (per Verizon DBIR)
Spear phishing uses OSINT (LinkedIn, social media) to personalize attacks
Common phishing indicators: urgent language, generic greetings, mismatched URLs, unexpected attachments, requests for credentials/payment
Phishing URLs often use typosquatted domains (amazom.com instead of amazon.com)
SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are email authentication protocols to combat phishing/spoofing
AiTM phishing kits (Evilginx, Modlishka) intercept both credentials and MFA tokens in real-time
FIDO2/WebAuthn is resistant to AiTM phishing because of origin binding
Report phishing to: your security team, anti-phishing working group (reportphishing@apwg.org)
topics.offense_application: Attackers use phishing as the primary initial access method: credential phishing (fake login pages), malware delivery (malicious attachments), MFA bypass (AiTM proxies), and lateral phishing (compromised account sends phishing to contacts).
topics.defense_application: Defenders implement email security (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), deploy secure email gateways, conduct phishing simulation training, enforce FIDO2 MFA (phishing-resistant), use URL rewriting and click-time analysis, and maintain clear reporting procedures.
drills: Analyze a phishing email: identify red flags, check headers, trace the sender's actual domain
Compare SPF, DKIM, and DMARC — explain how each combats email spoofing
Explain why FIDO2/WebAuthn is phishing-resistant but SMS and TOTP are not
common_mistakes: Relying on users to spot all phishing — technical controls (DMARC, secure email gateway) are essential
Punishing users who click phishing simulations — creates fear and underreporting; use positive reinforcement
Believing MFA stops phishing — AiTM phishing kits intercept MFA tokens; use phishing-resistant FIDO2

topics.title: Pretexting and Business Email Compromise (BEC)
concepts: Pretexting: creating a fabricated scenario (pretext) to obtain information or action from the target
Baiting: offering something enticing (free USB drive, download) to trick the victim
Quid pro quo: offering a benefit (tech support) in exchange for information/access
Tailgating/Piggybacking: following someone through a secure door without authorization
Business Email Compromise (BEC): compromising or impersonating business email to defraud the organization
BEC variants: CEO fraud, attorney impersonation, fake invoice, payroll diversion, W-2 theft
Watering hole attack: compromising a website the target group frequently visits
key_facts: BEC is the most financially damaging cybercrime category — FBI reports billions in losses annually
BEC commonly involves: compromised executive email accounts, lookalike domains, wire transfer fraud
CEO fraud: impersonating a CEO/executive to pressure employees into urgent wire transfers
Pretexting often combines OSINT research with social engineering techniques
Kevin Mitnick popularized social engineering in cybersecurity; his book 'The Art of Deception' is foundational
Watering hole attacks target industry-specific sites (e.g., a security conference website)
USB drop attacks: leaving infected USB drives in parking lots — human curiosity leads to insertion
topics.offense_application: Attackers use pretexting to build trust before exploitation, BEC to steal money directly (bypassing technical controls entirely by exploiting trust), watering hole attacks to compromise many targets at once, and USB drops for physical access.
topics.defense_application: Defenders implement financial transaction verification procedures (call-back verification for wire transfers), security awareness training, email authentication (DMARC), domain monitoring for lookalike domains, and physical security (badge access, mantraps).
drills: Analyze a BEC scenario: identify the red flags and what controls would have prevented it
Design a security awareness training module covering pretexting and BEC
Explain why BEC succeeds even when no technical vulnerability exists — it exploits human trust
common_mistakes: Thinking social engineering only targets technical staff — BEC targets finance and HR
Implementing only technical controls for BEC — process controls (call-back verification) are essential
Underestimating the financial impact of BEC — it exceeds ransomware in total reported losses

topics.title: Physical Security and Social Engineering Defense
concepts: Physical access = logical access: an attacker with physical access to a machine can often own it
Physical social engineering: tailgating, shoulder surfing, dumpster diving, badge cloning
USB drop attacks: malicious USB devices left in target areas (Rubber Ducky, Bash Bunny)
Security awareness training: educating employees to recognize and report social engineering
Security culture: embedding security mindset into organizational culture, not just annual training
Defense in depth for humans: technical controls + process controls + training + reporting
Red team social engineering: authorized simulations to test organizational resilience
key_facts: Physical attack tools: USB Rubber Ducky (keystroke injection), Bash Bunny, Hak5 gear, Proxmark3 (RFID cloning)
Evil twin / Rogue AP: setting up a fake Wi-Fi access point to capture credentials
Shoulder surfing: observing passwords/PINs being entered — mitigated by privacy screens
Dumpster diving: searching trash for documents with sensitive info — mitigated by shredding
Effective awareness training: short, frequent, relevant, scenario-based; not annual compliance videos
Positive reporting culture: reward employees for reporting suspicious activity, don't punish for falling for simulations
NIST SP 800-50: guidelines for building an IT security awareness and training program
topics.offense_application: Attackers exploit physical access (USB drops, rogue USB charging stations, Evil Twin Wi-Fi), use shoulder surfing and badge cloning for facility access, and exploit weak security culture to socially engineer their way past guards and receptionists.
topics.defense_application: Defenders implement physical security (badge access, mantraps, visitor logs), deploy endpoint controls (disable USB AutoRun, BitLocker, device control), build security awareness programs with frequent training, create easy reporting channels, and conduct authorized social engineering assessments.
drills: Design a security awareness program: list topics, frequency, format, and metrics for each audience
Identify physical security vulnerabilities in a sample office layout (badge access, visitor management, desk security)
Explain the difference between punitive and positive reporting cultures and why positive is more effective
common_mistakes: Treating security awareness as a compliance checkbox (annual video) rather than ongoing culture-building
Punishing employees who report clicking a suspicious link — discourages reporting of real incidents
Focusing only on digital social engineering — physical vectors (USB drops, badge cloning) are equally dangerous
